findings.claim: Studio One / Fender Studio Pro has an official, publicly documented scripting API or SDK for driving the DAW
findings.detail: There is no public DAW-automation API, SDK, or developer portal for Studio One. The only developer resource PreSonus (now Fender Digital) publishes is `presonus-plugin-extensions` on GitHub — host-specific *plug-in* extension headers that sit on top of the VST2/VST3/AU SDKs (e.g. Sound Variations, Instrument extensions in 5.2+, speaker-arrangement queries in 6.6+), shipped 'AS IS'. Its README explicitly says the actual SDKs 'are available separately from the owners of VST, VST3, and Audio Unit'. That repo is for people writing plug-ins, not for controlling the host. An r/StudioOne thread (2025-04-22) titled 'PreSonus Studio One 7 SDK' concludes that PreSonus 'does not currently offer a public API or SDK for extending the core DAW', with a commenter noting the developer portal covers ARA and the AudioLoop spec but nothing about Studio One itself. A Gearspace thread asking whether PreSonus ever released a proper API got the reply that they don't appear inclined to go that direction. Nothing in the Fender Studio Pro 8.0 / 8.1 / 8.2 release notes announces a scripting API. NOTE: presonus.com, fender.com, soundonsound.com and reaper.fm were blocked by this container's egress proxy (403 on CONNECT), so official pages were verified through search-engine extracts that quote them verbatim rather than by direct fetch.
findings.practical: Do not wait for an official API — there is none, and there is no sign one is coming. Plan around file exchange plus the MIDI-command trick below.

findings.claim: Studio One contains an undocumented internal JavaScript engine that third-party scripts can use
findings.detail: Studio One has shipped an embedded JavaScript scripting engine since version 4.5. It is real but completely undocumented by the vendor. A script ships as a ZIP renamed to `.package` containing at minimum three files: `metainfo.xml` (package metadata incl. a unique Package:ID), `classfactory.xml` (ScriptClass entries with unique classIDs, a sourceFile and functionName; menuPriority -1 hides the action from menus), and `code.js`. The community helper library is `DjFix/studioone_functions` (`functions.js`, 'functions include file for PreSonus Studio One 4.5 +', 14 stars, 181 commits), pulled in via `include_file('functions.js')` — and the README states 'The file is obfuscated and cannot be edited.' The exposed host surface includes `Host.GUI.Commands.interpretCommand` (fire any Studio One action by name), `Host.Interfaces.IEditTask`, `Host.Results.kResultOk`, plus track get/search/rename/select/colour/pan, mixer channel fader read/write (-144 to +10 dB), master fader, mute/solo, `setProgram` bank/program changes, and `loadCubasePatchFile`. A DJ TechTools poster who built mappings says there is 'zero documentation apart from what's in the existing scripts for the other manufacturers' and points at the `*.surface.xml` files under the Studio One `devices` subfolders as the only reference. A KVR thread 'Scripting in Studio One' shares a Windows helper app that generates script outlines and packages them.
findings.practical: This engine is the only real programmatic hook, and it is reverse-engineered, undocumented and can break with any update. Treat it as the foundation the community MCP servers stand on, not as something to build on yourself unless you enjoy that kind of work.

findings.claim: Third-party Studio One scripting add-ons exist, proving the extension path is open to developers
findings.detail: Add-ons exist, but the access appears privileged rather than open. Lukas Ruschitzka — described on his own Payhip seller page as a 'composer, keyboardist, and PreSonus Studio One product specialist' — developed 'Navigation Essentials', billed as 'the first official third-party scripting add-on for Studio One', distributed via his Studio One Toolbox service; he also sells 'Studio One Scoring Tools'. Other vendors' macro packs list 'Studio One Toolbox - Navigation Essentials' as a required dependency. However, the r/StudioOne SDK thread contains a commenter's account that his extensions rest on scripting access he obtained through his PreSonus working relationship — that is a community claim, not an official statement, and I could not verify it. There is no public application process, no documented extension API, and no published SDK.
findings.practical: The existence of these add-ons does not mean you can get the same access. Buy them as products if they help your workflow; do not read them as evidence that an open extension path exists.

findings.claim: Studio One's Macro Toolbar and macro commands are an official, supported feature
findings.detail: Macros are a first-class, shipped feature — and they are the most under-used automation lever in Studio One. Sound On Sound's 'Macro Machines' piece describes Macros as 'completely manipulable', letting you create your own pages, groups, menus and buttons, with a bundled library covering Music Editing and Music Creation tasks such as filtering and transposing notes. Workflow: click the Macro button, name it in the 'New Macro' dialog, then drag commands from the Command Palette into the Macro Editor's macro-body pane and save. Assign to a toolbar button by right-clicking the button and choosing 'Assign Macro'; 'Assign Command' instead lets you search and bind any command in Studio One. Macros are saved as `.studioonemacro` files, and the toolbar layout lives in a commandbar XML file in the Studio One user folder. Toolbars bundled with extensions are read-only. Caveat: several tutorial sites that surfaced in search are spun/low-quality copies disagreeing on the exact pane label ('Macro Body' vs 'Macro Physique'), so verify labels against your own version 8 UI.
findings.practical: This is where you get the most leverage for the least risk. Build one macro per repetitive step you want 'the AI' to trigger — e.g. select all notes on track / quantize / transpose / change instrument — and you have a stable, named command surface. Macros also survive updates far better than scripts.

findings.claim: There is a community MCP server for Studio One (searched: studio-one-mcp, studioone mcp, presonus mcp, fender studio mcp)
findings.detail: Two exist, both young and both built by individuals, neither affiliated with PreSonus/Fender. (1) `NeanderthalMan/studio-one-mcp` — JavaScript, MIT, 12 stars, 2 forks, 72 commits on main, created 2026-09-28, repo last updated 2026-10-20; published to npm as `studio-one-mcp`, latest 0.3.0 published 2026-09-30 (only two versions ever: 0.2.0, 0.3.0), requires Node >= 20. (2) `tiwadara/StudioOneMcp` — Python, 6 stars, 1 fork, 23 commits, 7-8 open issues, 1 open PR, created 2026-06-07, last updated 2026-10-18; self-described 'work in progress', MCP over JSON-RPC stdio. GitHub search for 'presonus studio one script' returns 0 repositories. Nothing exists under a 'fender studio mcp' name. A third project, `zarfld/presonus-studiolive-mcp`, is for StudioLive Series III *hardware mixers* (TCP 53000), not the DAW — do not confuse it.
findings.practical: They are real and surprisingly capable, but at 12 and 6 stars with weeks of history they are experiments, not products. Expect to debug them yourself.

findings.claim: studio-one-mcp can drive a running Studio One, including MIDI note editing, instruments and mixer
findings.detail: Its README is unusually candid: 'Studio One has no public API, no OSC, and no network scripting,' so it stacks two workarounds. `song_*` tools (song_list, song_read, song_history, song_diff) parse `.song` files directly — these are ZIP archives of XML — and need no running Studio One, but only reflect the last save/autosave. `live_*` tools go through an 'MCP Bridge' control-surface device installed into Studio One, running in the embedded JavaScript engine. Because that engine cannot open sockets, communication is a **file mailbox** (request.json / response.json / status.json). Because Studio One gives scripts no usable timer, the server rings a 'doorbell' by sending MIDI note 119 on a virtual MIDI port, resending every 150 ms until answered, 5 s timeout. Two companion extensions, 'MCP Edit' and 'MCP Track Edit', perform note edits as Studio One edit tasks without opening dialogs, and handle routing, folders, event renames and song-structure ops. Roughly 60 live tools incl. live_notes / live_edit_notes (transpose, velocity, quantize, move, delete, add), live_add_instrument_track, live_add_plugin, live_inserts, live_channels/live_set_channel, live_sends, live_plugin_params/live_set_plugin_param, live_markers, live_arranger, live_bounce, live_record, live_macros/live_run_macro, live_save/live_undo/live_redo, live_list_commands/live_command (~1,000 internal commands), and an opt-in live_eval.
findings.practical: Functionally this is close to what you want: it can read your piano MIDI in the live session, transpose it, and create an instrument track with a different plug-in. The architecture (file mailbox + MIDI doorbell) is clever but fragile — it is a workaround stack, not an integration.

findings.claim: These MCP servers work on Windows with Studio One 6/7 or Fender Studio Pro 8
findings.detail: Both are macOS projects with untested Windows support, and neither is tested on version 8. `studio-one-mcp` was developed against **Studio One 5.5.2 on macOS**; its README states paths for 'Studio One 6/7 and Studio Pro 8 are wired in but untested', and that Windows 'needs loopMIDI with a port named studio-one-mcp' and is likewise **untested**. Its doorbell mechanism relies on the macOS IAC Driver by default. `tiwadara/StudioOneMcp` states **Studio One 7 on macOS** as the only tested target, uses a CoreMIDI virtual port, and its menu-automation path uses macOS System Events requiring Accessibility permission — fundamentally non-portable. Its README says Windows/Linux 'would need a loopback MIDI driver such as loopMIDI or snd-virmidi'. Its own stated gaps: 224 mapped built-in commands verified end-to-end out of a 415-function catalogue (194 built-ins + 221 macros), and 139 user macros do not dispatch from a control surface at all (its issue #3).
findings.practical: On Windows + Studio Pro 8 you would be the first person testing this. If you try studio-one-mcp, install loopMIDI first, create a port named exactly `studio-one-mcp`, and run `npx -y studio-one-mcp doctor`. Budget an evening for it to not work, and have the file-exchange workflow as your actual plan.

findings.claim: Even a working Studio One MCP server would let this cloud Claude session control the DAW
findings.detail: This session runs in a Linux cloud container with no access to the user's Windows disk or MIDI ports. Both MCP servers are local processes that must run on the same machine as Studio One: they write to a local mailbox folder and open a local virtual MIDI port. `studio-one-mcp setup` registers itself with Claude Code and optionally Claude Desktop **on that machine**. So the MCP route requires a Claude that runs locally — the Claude Desktop app, or `claude remote-control` in a terminal in the working folder, which then appears in the Claude Code app. A cloud session can only be bridged by the user explicitly starting Remote Control from a trusted device.
findings.practical: Decide this first, because it splits the whole plan: if you want live DAW control, you must run Claude locally on the Windows machine (Claude Desktop or `claude remote-control`). If you keep working in this cloud session, the loop is upload/download MIDI files — which works today and needs no setup.

findings.claim: Studio One's MIDI Learn / 'Assign Command' is an officially documented way to fire any Studio One command from outside
findings.detail: This is the officially supported automation backbone, and it is what both MCP servers exploit. PreSonus KB 'MIDI Transport Control Assignment (MIDI Learn)' instructs: if transport buttons don't work, 'enable MMC commands on the device, or use the MIDI Learn feature to learn the controls and assign them to Studio One Commands.' Sweetwater's tutorial documents the general form: right-click a hardware button, click 'Assign Command', which opens the keyboard-shortcuts window, then search for any command and bind it. Separately, **Control Link** binds hardware controls to plug-in/mixer parameters: move the software control with the mouse, move the hardware control, click Assign — with Global mapping (fixed 1:1) and Focus mapping (follows the focused plug-in window). Prerequisite: the controller must first be added under Preferences/Options > External Devices, via [New Control Surface] for generic gear, with 'Receive From' set to the MIDI port; for a new generic device all MIDI CCs are active and shown as knobs. Known weakness: a Waves forum user reported Control Link mappings to plug-ins being lost after switching plug-ins and returning (Focus-mode behaviour).
findings.practical: This is the cheapest reliable automation you have, and it needs no MCP server at all. Install loopMIDI, create a virtual port, add it as a New Control Surface, then MIDI-Learn CC messages onto the commands and macros you care about. Anything that can send a MIDI CC — including a tiny local script — can then trigger those commands.

findings.claim: Studio One supports OSC (Open Sound Control)
findings.detail: No evidence of OSC support in any Studio One version. Targeted searching for Studio One + OSC returned nothing on the subject; every result was about the Studio One Remote app instead. The `studio-one-mcp` author, who reverse-engineered the scripting engine, states flatly in the README: 'Studio One has no public API, no OSC, and no network scripting.' This is the sharpest contrast with Ableton, where community MCP servers rely on AbletonOSC. Marked refuted rather than unverifiable because the absence is asserted directly by the one developer who went looking, and no OSC preference pane, port setting or KB article exists.
findings.practical: Rule out every OSC-based automation idea, and with it the whole class of tooling (TouchOSC, Open Stage Control, AbletonOSC-style bridges) that other DAWs get for free.

findings.claim: Studio One has a network remote-control protocol (UCNET) that could be driven programmatically
findings.detail: The protocol exists but is closed and, for the DAW specifically, not publicly reverse-engineered. Studio One Remote (free iPad app, App Store id988444520, released July 2015; Android version added 2017) is 'based on PreSonus' UCNET protocol for fast, reliable network connectivity and remote control', the same stack behind UC Surface, QMix-UC and Capture. It can control any Studio One Professional instance on the same network, and multiple remotes can attach to one Studio One simultaneously; it exposes transport, mix console, Macro Controls and Commands. Crucially: **the reverse-engineering work that exists targets StudioLive hardware mixers, not the DAW** — `featherbear/presonus-studiolive-api` (TypeScript) explores the StudioLive Series III network control protocol, and `zarfld/presonus-studiolive-mcp` (v0.1.0, experimental, read-mostly, validated on a StudioLive 32SC firmware 3.3.0.109659) documents TCP port 53000 as the 'UC Surface / Studio One Remote protocol'. No packet format, handshake, port or third-party client for the Studio One DAW side turned up in any search.
findings.practical: Interesting but a dead end for you. The fact that the app exposes 'Commands' and Macro Controls over the network means a clean integration is technically possible — but somebody would have to reverse-engineer the DAW side first, and nobody has published that.

findings.claim: Studio One supports ReWire
findings.detail: ReWire is gone. PreSonus's Studio One 6 support section lists a starred article '★ ReWire Discontinuation Notice for Studio One 6', so version 6 is where it was dropped — which means it is absent from 6, 7 and Fender Studio Pro 8. Version 5 did support it: launch copy advertised 'VST / AU and ReWire' and a Studio One 5 KB article covers ReWire startup errors and tells users to 'Disable the ReWire service in the Studio One preferences under Advanced > Services'. This matches the industry-wide picture, as Reason Studios ended ReWire development. I could not read the discontinuation notice itself (presonus.com blocked by this container's proxy), so the stated reason is unverified; the version boundary is confirmed by the article title.
findings.practical: Forget ReWire as a bridge. It would not have helped much anyway — it carried audio and transport sync, not editing commands.

findings.claim: Studio One exposes a named-pipe or socket interface for local IPC
findings.detail: No. The `studio-one-mcp` README states the embedded JavaScript engine 'cannot open sockets', which is precisely why the author resorted to a filesystem mailbox (request.json / response.json / status.json) plus a MIDI note as a doorbell, with 150 ms resends because the engine also exposes no usable timer. There is no documented named pipe, no local HTTP server, no CLI with a scripting entry point. The only network listener is the closed UCNET service for the Remote app.
findings.practical: Any integration you build will be file-polling plus MIDI triggers. That is the ceiling, and it is why both existing MCP servers look the way they do.

findings.claim: REAPER offers official scripting (ReaScript) in Lua/Python plus mature community MCP servers
findings.detail: Yes, and the gap is enormous. REAPER ships ReaScript as a documented, first-party API: scripts can be written in EEL2, Lua, or Python; Lua and EEL2 are built in, while Python must be installed separately and enabled in preferences (with some UI features unavailable from Python). The official generated reference (reaper.fm/sdk/reascript/reascripthelp.html, generated from v7.35) covers the C/C++ API and all scripting languages. A documentation MCP server, `reaper-dev-mcp`, reports **2,282 functions** across C/EEL2/Lua/Python. Control-oriented servers: `shiehn/total-reaper-mcp` (Lua bridge inside REAPER + Python MCP server, file-based IPC, requires REAPER 6.83+ and Python 3.10+, profiles from ~15 to 600+ tools, default 'dsl-production' profile 53 tools); `bonfire-audio/reaper-mcp` (58 tools: project, tracks, MIDI, FX, mixing, mastering, rendering, audio analysis, via python-reapy with REAPER's distant API enabled); `xdarkzx-reaper-mcp` on PyPI (173 tools, Lua bridge, file-based IPC). Note that even REAPER's MCP servers use a Lua bridge with file IPC — but there it is built on a documented API rather than a reverse-engineered one.
findings.practical: If agent-driven DAW work ever becomes the point rather than a nice-to-have, REAPER is the answer — it is cheap ($60 personal licence) and you can run it alongside Studio One, not instead of it.

findings.claim: Ableton Live offers the Live Object Model plus community MCP servers (AbletonMCP)
findings.detail: Confirmed, with several competing implementations. The original is `ahujasid/ableton-mcp`, which drives Live through **AbletonOSC**, a free Remote Script exposing Live's API over the network; its tools are fixed per-action commands. Forks took it further: one adds a Remote Script opening a JSON-over-TCP socket server dispatching to handler modules that call the Live Object Model directly, split by domain (session, tracks, clips, devices, browser). `opendining/ableton-mcp-server` takes a 'Code Mode' approach inspired by Cloudflare — instead of predefined commands the agent writes and executes Python directly inside Live's runtime, with tools to read, write and call properties on Live objects. Several other Ableton MCP servers exist on registries. The enabling difference versus Studio One: Live ships a documented Python Remote Script layer with network exposure.
findings.practical: Same conclusion as REAPER — Ableton is a genuinely agent-controllable DAW. Not worth switching to for your use case, but it explains why Studio One tooling is so thin.

findings.claim: PreSonus Studio One was rebranded as Fender Studio Pro, with version 8 the first release under the new name
findings.detail: Confirmed and consistent across Sound On Sound, MusicTech, Macworld, Mixdown and Synth Anatomy. The change took effect **13 January 2026**: Studio One became **Fender Studio Pro**, Quantum became the Fender Quantum Series, AudioBox became Fender AudioBox. Fender had acquired PreSonus in **November 2021**. Fender took over all licensing, subscriptions and support; accounts migrated from MyPreSonus to the new **MyFender** platform. The PreSonus brand continues for hardware (Eris monitors, StudioLive Series III SE mixers, Air XD loudspeakers). Version 8 headline additions: Mustang Native and Rumble Native plug-ins (57 guitar/bass amp models plus hundreds of effects, exclusive to Fender Studio and Studio Pro), a new Studio Verb reverb, an Arrangement Overview, an expanded Chord Track with a Chord Assistant that recommends chords from an existing progression, and AI-based audio-to-MIDI. One reviewer notes the rename costs search visibility, since years of 'Studio One' tutorials and reviews no longer match the product name.
findings.practical: Practical consequence for you: when searching for help, search 'Studio One' — not 'Fender Studio Pro'. Almost all tutorials, macros, scripts and forum answers still use the old name, and the underlying app is the same lineage.

findings.claim: The downloaded build is Fender Studio Pro 8 version 8.2.0.114903
findings.detail: The 8.2 release is confirmed; the exact four-part build string is not. Fender's newsroom post 'Fender Studio Pro 8.2 Expands Mixing and Creative Production Tools' is dated **20 October 2026**, with Mix Online coverage 21 October 2026 — six days before today, so a fresh download being 8.2 is entirely consistent. 8.2 is a free update for Fender Studio Pro+ subscribers and qualifying perpetual licence holders. Confirmed 8.2 features: **Trim Automation** (a volume trim layer on a channel or send, so you can change level without redrawing existing automation), **Dim Solo Mode** (dims other channels instead of muting, keeping already-muted channels muted), **Multiple Marker Tracks** (each settable to time or bar/beat), extended Stem Separation adding guitar and piano isolation, Vocal Tune Low Latency mode (reportedly under 3 ms) and a Follow option, **Per Note Sound Variations** (attach an articulation to an individual note), and **MIDI 2.0 support** — with the caveat that Windows users must wait for Microsoft's official MIDI 2.0 release, which Fender says needs **Windows 11 25H2 or later**. The specific build number 114903 appears in no source I could reach; I could not fetch Fender's own version page. Note the coincidental resemblance to the StudioLive firmware 3.3.0.109659 cited elsewhere — Fender/PreSonus use this build-number style, so the string is plausible, just unverified.
findings.practical: You are on the newest release, which is good news: Per Note Sound Variations and the expanded Chord Track are both directly useful for what you want to do. If you care about MIDI 2.0, check you are on Windows 11 25H2 or later.

findings.claim: Fender Studio Pro 8 can convert a recorded performance into editable MIDI natively
findings.detail: Yes — and this is the single most useful fact for a manual-composition workflow. Version 8 added two audio-to-MIDI functions: **Extract Notes** and **Extract Beats**, each based on its own model. Extract Notes handles monophonic *and* polyphonic tuned instruments; Extract Beats is trained on acoustic drums. Both place extracted data on a new Instrument Track assigned to Mai Tai or Impact, and the user can swap in any virtual instrument afterwards. Retailers describe it as one-click conversion of a recorded performance into editable MIDI. A later 8.x update improved audio-to-note accuracy. Version 8 also added the expanded **Chord Track with Chord Assistant**, which recommends chords based on an existing progression. These are deterministic analysis tools applied to the user's own performance — they transcribe what the human played, they do not generate new musical content.
findings.practical: This changes your workflow: you can hum, play, or beatbox a part and have Studio One transcribe it to MIDI that you then edit. Combined with the Chord Track, most of what you wanted from 'AI help' is already inside the DAW, with no copyright ambiguity — it is your performance, transcribed.

findings.claim: Fender Studio Pro's built-in 'Studio Assistant' can act as an agent that composes or edits in the DAW
findings.detail: No — it is a documentation and guidance chatbot, not a DAW-driving agent. Introduced in **8.1**, Studio Assistant is a natural-language in-DAW helper that 'brings documentation, tutorials and support into one place' and searches Studio Pro documentation and online resources to answer questions without breaking workflow; Fender markets it as an 'intelligent in-DAW guide for real-time answers, creative direction and technical support'. It is available only as a **public beta for Fender Studio Pro+ users**. Nothing in Fender's press release, Sound On Sound, Premier Guitar, MusicTech or Mixdown coverage describes it editing MIDI, creating tracks, or executing commands. Separately, 8.1 added a **Moises Studio integration** for stem separation, vocal transformation and backing-track generation (free tier: 10 stem separations, 120 stem generations, 5 voice conversions per month) plus a native Vocal Tune plug-in — the backing-track generation there *is* generative AI and is the one feature to avoid if human authorship matters to you. Reporting on the assistant's accuracy and pricing beyond Pro+ is unverified.
findings.practical: Do not count on Studio Assistant to do the work — it answers 'how do I...' questions. And steer clear of Moises backing-track *generation* specifically; stem separation and vocal tuning applied to your own recording are fine, generated backing tracks are not if you want clean sole authorship.

findings.claim: MIDI files can be exchanged reliably between Studio One and an external assistant
findings.detail: Yes, with one important gotcha. Export: PreSonus's MIDI FAQ says use **File > Save As** and choose .mid / .midi — this route preserves the **tempo map and song markers**, which other export paths drop. Studio One writes **Type 1 (multitrack) MIDI only, not Type 0**. A faster but lossier alternative is dragging to the Browser's **Files** tab ('arguably one of the most efficient ways', though 'it may not carry the full file attributes'). **Gotcha: Studio One does not support dragging and dropping out to Windows Explorer / macOS Finder** — a Toontrack forum thread documents this, with the Files tab as the workaround. Import: Studio One 6+ accepts a MIDI file 'of any size' dropped into an existing song without opening a new song. Plug-in-specific drag behaviour varies (e.g. with Maschine, a plain drag puts each pad on a separate track while holding Ctrl places pads sequentially on one track), so test with your own instruments.
findings.practical: This is your working loop, available right now with zero setup: File > Save As > .mid, upload the file here, I read and edit it, you drag the result back into the arrangement. Use Save As rather than drag-out, both because drag-to-Explorer does not work and because Save As keeps your tempo and markers intact — which matters when parts have to line up.

research.recommendation:
BOTTOM LINE: Studio One / Fender Studio Pro is one of the worst mainstream DAWs for agent control, and nothing about version 8 changes that. No public API, no SDK, no OSC, no sockets, no ReWire (dropped at v6). The only programmatic hook is an undocumented, reverse-engineered embedded JavaScript engine that cannot even open a socket or set a timer. Two community MCP servers do exist — NeanderthalMan/studio-one-mcp (JS, npm 0.3.0, ~60 live tools, MIT) and tiwadara/StudioOneMcp (Python, WIP) — and they are genuinely impressive, but both are macOS-only in practice, both are weeks old with 12 and 6 stars, and neither is tested on Windows or on version 8. For this user specifically there is a second, harder blocker: those servers run locally next to Studio One, so this cloud session cannot use them at all. Live DAW control would require running Claude on the Windows machine (Claude Desktop, or `claude remote-control` in a terminal).

RECOMMENDED PLAN — do not chase MCP first. Three layers, in order of payoff per unit of pain:

1. MIDI FILE EXCHANGE (works today, zero setup, the actual answer). The user plays the piano parts themselves in Studio One, then File > Save As > .mid (NOT drag-to-Explorer, which Studio One does not support; Save As is also the only route that preserves the tempo map and markers). Upload the .mid here. The assistant reads it, writes drum/bass/string parts or reassigns instruments, returns a .mid, and the user drags it into the arrangement. Note Studio One writes Type 1 multitrack MIDI only. This loop is reliable, version-proof, and leaves authorship unambiguous.

2. IN-DAW TOOLS THE USER ALREADY OWNS (strongly under-appreciated). Version 8's Extract Notes (mono AND polyphonic) and Extract Beats (trained on acoustic drums) transcribe the user's own performance to MIDI in one click — so they can play or beatbox a part rather than program it. The expanded Chord Track with Chord Assistant suggests chords from an existing progression. 8.2 adds Per Note Sound Variations for per-note articulation. Macros are the other big lever: build one macro per repetitive step (select notes on track / quantize / transpose / swap instrument), saved as .studioonemacro, assigned to toolbar buttons. Macros survive updates far better than scripts.

3. MIDI-TRIGGERED COMMANDS (the officially supported automation path, no MCP needed). Install loopMIDI, add the virtual port under Options > External Devices as a New Control Surface, then use MIDI Learn / right-click > 'Assign Command' to bind CCs to any Studio One command or macro. Anything that can send a CC can then fire those commands. This is exactly the mechanism both MCP servers exploit, minus the fragility.

Only if the user genuinely wants live control: run Claude locally on Windows, install loopMIDI with a port named exactly `studio-one-mcp`, run `npx -y studio-one-mcp setup` then `doctor`, add studio-one-mcp > MCP Bridge under External Devices (Receive From = the virtual port, Send To = None), restart Studio One. Warn them they are the first Windows + v8 tester, leave `--allow-eval` off, and note the README's own warnings: unreliable undo for mixer/mute/rename/color/add-send, modal Scripting Error dialogs that silently break edits, markers only 1-20, no envelope-point writing, and a dropped notification-API feature that crashed Studio One three times.

COPYRIGHT ANGLE (the user's explicit requirement): the recommended plan is clean. The human plays every part; Extract Notes/Beats merely transcribes their own performance; the assistant's role is arrangement suggestions and mechanical MIDI transformation that the human reviews and accepts in the DAW. Two things to flag: (a) the 8.1 Moises integration's backing-track GENERATION is generative AI and should be avoided — stem separation and vocal tuning on their own recording are fine; (b) Studio Assistant (8.1, Pro+ beta) is only a documentation Q&A chatbot, so it is irrelevant both as a tool and as an authorship concern. Separately: the "Iron Man" reference in the user's request points at a copyrighted film score — the parent agent should steer this toward an original piece in a similar style (ostinato brass/strings, driving low end) rather than reproducing that cue.

ALSO WORTH SAYING: if agent-driven production ever becomes the point rather than a bonus, REAPER is the right tool — first-party ReaScript in Lua/Python/EEL2, 2,282 documented functions, and several mature MCP servers (total-reaper-mcp up to 600+ tools, bonfire-audio/reaper-mcp 58 tools). At ~$60 it can sit alongside Studio One as the 'automation workbench' rather than replacing it. Ableton is the other agent-friendly option via the Live Object Model and AbletonOSC-based servers.

CAVEAT ON SOURCING: this container's egress proxy returned 403 for presonus.com, fender.com, soundonsound.com and reaper.fm, so official pages were verified through search-engine extracts quoting them verbatim rather than by direct fetch. GitHub, raw.githubusercontent.com and the npm registry were reachable and were read directly. The build string 8.2.0.114903 could not be verified against any source — the 8.2 release itself (20 Oct 2026) is confirmed. The claim that Lukas Ruschitzka's scripting access came via his PreSonus relationship is a community account, not an official statement.

verdicts.claim: Studio One / Fender Studio Pro has an official, publicly documented scripting API or SDK for driving the DAW
verdicts.reason: The finding's refutation holds, and I confirmed it with two sources independent of the cited repo and of the Reddit thread. (a) The community-built CSources/Studio-Pro-Scripting-API-Reference states verbatim: 'Fender/PreSonus does not provide official public documentation for this API' and 'The API is internal and undocumented.' (b) A thread on studiooneforum.com ('Studio One - Scripting API') has a PreSonus-affiliated moderator stating there is no public documentation or official support for scripting. I also read the presonus-plugin-extensions README directly (github.com HTML, since raw/main 404s): it is plug-in-side headers only (ipsl*.h, pslvst2extensions.h), 35 stars, default branch main. Three corrections, none of which change the verdict: (1) the finding presents a quotation that is not verbatim — the README actually says 'These technologies are maintained by their respective owners and the appropriate SDKs are available separately', not 'available separately from the owners of VST, VST3, and Audio Unit'; (2) the flat statement that the repo 'is for people writing plug-ins, not for controlling the host' is slightly overstated — one listed feature is 'Remote control channel volume, mute, solo, etc. from plug-in', i.e. an officially published way for a plug-in to act on host mixer channels, though still not external DAW automation; (3) 'no developer portal' is too strong — PreSonus's Linux Getting Started KB article refers plug-in developers to 'the PreSonus developer page' for new plug-in-GUI APIs, so a developer page does exist; it just does not cover DAW scripting. presonus.com, fender.com, soundonsound.com, reaper.fm, payhip.com, kvraudio.com, reddit.com and github.io are DNS-blocked for both curl and WebFetch in this container, so those were verified only through search-engine extracts quoting them.
verdicts.corrected_value: A PreSonus/Fender developer page does exist (plug-in GUI APIs, ARA, AudioLoop) — it simply contains no DAW-automation API. The plug-in extensions do include plug-in-side remote control of host channel volume/mute/solo. The README quote in the finding is a paraphrase, not verbatim.

verdicts.claim: Studio One contains an undocumented internal JavaScript engine that third-party scripts can use
verdicts.reason: Confirmed, and I verified the specifics directly rather than through the finding's summary. DjFix/studioone_functions matches exactly what was claimed: 14 stars, 2 forks, 181 commits, About text 'functions include file for PreSonus Studio One 4.5 +', and the README states verbatim 'The file is obfuscated and cannot be edited.' Host.GUI.Commands.interpretCommand("category","action"), Host.Interfaces.IEditTask and Host.Results.kResultOk are all present, as is include_file('functions.js') and the -144 to 10 dB fader range. Two corrections: (1) the finding lists setProgram and loadCubasePatchFile as part of 'the exposed host surface' — they are helper functions provided by functions.js itself, not Host API members (setProgram sets bank/program for an external instrument; loadCubasePatchFile parses a Cubase patch .txt file); (2) the practical note that there is 'zero documentation apart from what's in the existing scripts' is now out of date — CSources/Studio-Pro-Scripting-API-Reference (7 stars, 3 forks, 21 commits, main, a Docusaurus site) is a community reference covering package structure (metainfo.xml, classfactory.xml), script types, the Host API, the context object, and Event/Region/Track/Channel/Mixer/Time objects, with a 'Known Limitations & Open Items' section (no MIDI CC iteration, context.mainTrackList undefined in MusicEdit, selection not undoable). It is community-derived, incomplete, and was itself written with help from coding agents, so treat it as a map rather than a spec.
verdicts.corrected_value: A community scripting API reference now exists that the finding missed: github.com/CSources/Studio-Pro-Scripting-API-Reference. setProgram and loadCubasePatchFile are functions.js helpers, not host API members.

verdicts.claim: Third-party Studio One scripting add-ons exist, proving the extension path is open to developers
verdicts.reason: The assessment holds — add-ons exist, and the access looks privileged rather than open — and independent sources actually strengthen the privileged-access reading: Ruschitzka's own profile describes him not only as a PreSonus Studio One product specialist but as having created the MIDI editing functions in Studio One 4.5, i.e. he wrote part of the shipping product. The 'first official third-party scripting add-on' billing remains self-reported on his own product and profile pages; no independent source corroborates 'first'. No public application process, extension API or SDK surfaced. Two factual corrections that matter for the user's next action: (1) Navigation Essentials is FREE, not a product to buy — the finding's practical advice to 'buy them as products' is wrong; Ruschitzka has described it as the free/demo version of his paid Scoring Tools, with some commands (Volume, Pan, Select by Color) appearing only in the free version; (2) the canonical pages are s1toolbox.com/navigationessentials and manual.studioonescripts.com/navigationessentials, not the payhip URL cited. Most usefully, Navigation Essentials states compatibility with Fender Studio Pro 8, Studio One Pro 7, Studio One 6 and Studio One 5 (5.5.2+), and adds 30+ features including track management, volume/pan control and note editing — so vendor-independent scripting demonstrably does work on version 8, which is more than can be said for the MCP servers.
verdicts.corrected_value: Navigation Essentials is free, not paid, and explicitly supports Fender Studio Pro 8 / Studio One Pro 7 / 6 / 5.5.2+. Canonical URL: s1toolbox.com/navigationessentials.

verdicts.claim: Studio One's Macro Toolbar and macro commands are an official, supported feature
verdicts.reason: The headline claim is solidly confirmed — the Macro Toolbar is a shipped, first-class feature with its own PreSonus Q&A entries ('What is the macro tool bar in Studio One?'), a bundled preset library, and user-creatable pages, groups, menus and buttons. The storage detail also checks out: a vi-control thread puts the toolbar layout at 'Studio One/Macros/commandbar-v3.xml' (older versions: CommandBar.xml), matching the finding's 'commandbar XML file in the Studio One user folder'. However, the specific UI mechanics in the finding are not independently verifiable and partly do not match what I could find: targeted searching turned up no source for a 'Command Palette', a 'Macro Editor' macro-body pane, or the '.studioonemacro' file extension. What independent sources do describe is a Macro Toolbar hidden by default, opened via the icon to the right of the 'Q' button or the View menu, with a 'Macro Organizer' for adding macros and their commands, and right-click in the macro bar to create groups and buttons. The finding's own caveat was right — the 'Macro Body' vs 'Macro Physique' disagreement is a tell that those sources were machine-spun copies, and 'Macro Physique' is a mistranslation artifact, not a real pane name. The practical advice (build one macro per repetitive step to get a stable named command surface) stands regardless of label accuracy.
verdicts.corrected_value: Verify labels in the version 8 UI. The official-looking term found independently is 'Macro Organizer', not 'Macro Editor'/'Command Palette'; the '.studioonemacro' extension is not independently verifiable. Toolbar layout file: Studio One/Macros/commandbar-v3.xml.

verdicts.claim: There is a community MCP server for Studio One (searched: studio-one-mcp, studioone mcp, presonus mcp, fender studio mcp)
verdicts.reason: Confirmed, with every metadata figure independently reproduced. GitHub repository search returned NeanderthalMan/studio-one-mcp: JavaScript, MIT, 12 stars, 2 forks, created 2026-09-28, pushed 2026-09-30, updated 2026-10-20 — all matching. And tiwadara/StudioOneMcp: Python, 6 stars, 1 fork, created 2026-06-07, updated 2026-10-18 — also matching. The npm registry independently corroborates the publishing history: package studio-one-mcp has only ever had two versions, 0.2.0 (2026-09-29) and 0.3.0 (2026-09-30), latest 0.3.0, engines node >=20, MIT. Unverifiable (api.github.com is gated for these repos in this session): the '72 commits on main' figure, and tiwadara's '23 commits, 7-8 open issues, 1 open PR'. One detail worth adding to the finding's 'these are experiments' conclusion: studio-one-mcp's pushed_at is 2026-09-30, so there has been no code pushed in roughly four weeks even though the repo's updated_at is 2026-10-20 — the later timestamp reflects metadata, not development. The npm package likewise has had no release in four weeks.
verdicts.corrected_value: studio-one-mcp has had no code pushed since 2026-09-30 (pushed_at) and no npm release since 0.3.0 on 2026-09-30, despite updated_at of 2026-10-20.

verdicts.claim: studio-one-mcp can drive a running Studio One, including MIDI note editing, instruments and mixer
verdicts.reason: Confirmed; I read the README directly and the architecture is as described, verbatim in several places. 'Studio One has no public API, no OSC, and no network scripting.' The song_* layer 'Parse[s] .song files, which are zip archives of XML', needs no running Studio One, and reflects only 'the last save or autosave' (song_list even includes autosave-only songs). The live_* layer goes through an in-app bridge device in the embedded SpiderMonkey engine; 'Scripts can read and write files but cannot open sockets', hence the file mailbox, and the doorbell is MIDI note 119 resent 'every 150 ms until answered (5 s timeout)', with the client polling response.json every 20 ms. Tool names check out: live_notes, live_edit_notes, live_add_instrument_track, live_add_plugin, live_inserts, live_plugin_params, live_set_plugin_param, live_macros, live_run_macro, live_command, live_list_commands, and live_eval which is opt-in behind --allow-eval. Companion extensions confirmed: MCP Edit (note editing, and notably it 'applies only a fixed set of operations, never code from the mailbox') and MCP Track Edit (output routing, moving tracks into folders, renaming events). Corrections: the tool count is 57 total — 53 live_ tools and 4 song_ tools — not 'roughly 60 live tools'; and the mailbox is larger than stated, adding edit-request.json / edit-result.json / track-edit-request.json / track-edit-result.json alongside status.json / request.json / response.json. The default mailbox path is the macOS '~/Library/Application Support/studio-one-mcp', which is further evidence for the macOS-first concern in the next finding.
verdicts.corrected_value: 57 tools total: 53 live_ and 4 song_, not ~60 live tools. Mailbox also includes edit-request.json, edit-result.json, track-edit-request.json, track-edit-result.json. Default mailbox path is macOS-specific.

verdicts.claim: These MCP servers work on Windows with Studio One 6/7 or Fender Studio Pro 8
verdicts.reason: The refutation holds and the two key sentences are verbatim as quoted. studio-one-mcp: 'Developed against Studio One 5.5.2 on macOS' and 'Paths for Windows and for Studio One 6/7 and Studio Pro 8 are wired in but untested.' Windows needs loopMIDI with a port named studio-one-mcp; the default MIDI port is 'the first MIDI output whose name contains IAC' unless STUDIO_ONE_MCP_MIDI_PORT is set — a macOS-specific default, as the finding said. The doctor command is real: 'npx -y studio-one-mcp doctor' and it 'checks every link in the chain and tells you how to fix the first broken one.' tiwadara/StudioOneMcp: its four control paths were each 'proven to work on Studio One 7 (macOS)', it is self-described as 'Community project, work in progress', not affiliated with PreSonus, opens a CoreMIDI virtual port, and for Windows/Linux points to 'a loopback such as loopMIDI / snd-virmidi named StudioOneMCP'. Counts confirmed: 194 built-in commands + 221 macros = 415 functions, 224 mapped commands, and 139 user macros in docs/macros-todo.json that do not dispatch from a control surface. Three qualifications: (1) tiwadara's port name is StudioOneMCP, different from studio-one-mcp's studio-one-mcp, so the two are not interchangeable; (2) its macOS System Events path is optional rather than mandatory, so 'fundamentally non-portable' overstates how load-bearing it is; (3) '224 mapped built-in commands verified end-to-end' is stronger than the README supports — it says the MIDI-to-command path is confirmed working and gives one worked example (Add Audio Track). The 'issue #3' attribution is unverifiable here (GitHub issues API gated). Worth noting for the user: scripting itself does work on version 8 (Navigation Essentials supports it); it is specifically these MCP servers that are untested there.
verdicts.corrected_value: tiwadara's MIDI port must be named StudioOneMCP, not studio-one-mcp. Its System Events dependency is optional. The '224 verified end-to-end' figure is stronger than the README states.

verdicts.claim: Even a working Studio One MCP server would let this cloud Claude session control the DAW
verdicts.reason: Correctly refuted, and I verified the environment side directly rather than inferring it. This container is Linux (kernel 6.18.44-fc-v153, x86_64); there is no NTFS/CIFS/SMB/9p/drvfs mount and no /mnt/<drive> of any kind, so the user's Windows disk is not reachable; and there is no /dev/snd and no ALSA sequencer (aconnect absent), so there are no MIDI ports at all — the doorbell mechanism could not be driven from here even in principle. The README side agrees: the default mailbox is a local path under the user's own profile, the live_* tools require a running Studio One, and the README warns that 'anything running as your user can drive Studio One through the mailbox' while advising 'Keep the folder local' — all of which presume one machine. setup registers the server with Claude Code and optionally Claude Desktop on that machine. The README does not state the same-machine requirement in so many words, so that specific sentence is an inference, but a sound one. The finding's split-the-plan conclusion is right and is the most consequential item in the set. One incidental note: Fender Studio Pro does have a Linux build (PreSonus publishes a 'Linux - Getting Started' article, and 8.2's MIDI 2.0 currently works on macOS and Linux), but that does not create a path here — this container has no audio device, no display and no licence.
verdicts.corrected_value: Verified directly in this container: Linux, no Windows/host mounts, no /dev/snd, no ALSA sequencer, so no MIDI ports — the bridge is impossible from here, not merely unsupported.

verdicts.claim: Studio One's MIDI Learn / 'Assign Command' is an officially documented way to fire any Studio One command from outside
verdicts.reason: Confirmed, and corroborated by a second official KB article the finding did not cite: 'MIDI: External Devices/Control Surfaces Setup' (support.presonus.com/hc/en-us/articles/210040463), alongside a more general 'MIDI: Transport Control Assignment & MIDI Learn' article. The documented mechanism is real: add the controller under External Devices, open Console/Mixer view, click External, double-click the device to open a MIDI Learn window, press the physical control so it populates the list, then right-click the control and choose Assign / 'assign command' and search for any Studio One command to bind. Control Link and the MMC prerequisite for transport buttons are also corroborated. One correction: the finding says 'Assign Command' 'opens the keyboard-shortcuts window' — that is not corroborated. Keyboard shortcuts are a separate route (Options > General > Keyboard Shortcuts on Windows, Preferences on macOS), and the Assign flow presents its own command search box. The practical advice — loopMIDI port, add as New Control Surface, MIDI-Learn CCs onto commands and macros — is sound and remains the cheapest reliable automation. Useful addition for the user: Help > Keyboard Shortcuts renders an HTML list of every currently configured key command, which is the fastest way to inventory the command names worth binding. Caveat the sources themselves raise: the MIDI Learn article is roughly five years old and menu names drift between versions and platforms.
verdicts.corrected_value: 'Assign Command' opens its own command search box, not the keyboard-shortcuts window; keyboard shortcuts are a separate route under Options/Preferences > Keyboard Shortcuts.

verdicts.claim: Studio One supports OSC (Open Sound Control)
verdicts.reason: The refutation now rests on a primary source independent of the studio-one-mcp author, which is what this claim most needed. PreSonus's own community Q&A, 'Is there "open sound control" support in Studio One?' (answers.presonus.com/4112), states that Studio One is not supported for OSC, and a later answer in the same thread points to OSC as a most-viewed, highest-voted feature request — i.e. the vendor's own forum treats it as absent and wanted. The same thread describes workarounds involving loopback drivers to get something TouchOSC-like working. Independently, a Behringer-forum user reports that because Studio One does not support OSC they routed OSC-to-MIDI and used MIDI CC instead — exactly the fallback the finding recommends. TouchOSC's own materials list Logic Pro as an officially supported control-surface target and do not list Studio One. No OSC preference pane, port setting or KB article surfaced in any search. So this is no longer resting on one developer's assertion. The one caveat the sources carry is age: the PreSonus Q&A dates from 2016 with a 2021 follow-up, so nothing here speaks directly to version 8, though no 8.x release-notes coverage mentions OSC either.
verdicts.corrected_value: Now independently confirmed by PreSonus's own Q&A forum rather than only the studio-one-mcp README — the finding can be stated with more confidence than it was.

verdicts.claim: Studio One has a network remote-control protocol (UCNET) that could be driven programmatically
verdicts.reason: The assessment holds: the protocol is real, it is closed, and the DAW side is not publicly reverse-engineered. Independent coverage (Sweetwater InSync, fast-and-wide, MusicRadar, Synthtopia) confirms Studio One Remote is built on PreSonus's UCNET networking technology, the same stack as UC Surface and Capture, requires the Studio One machine to be on the same network, and allows several tablets to control one instance. Crucially for the finding's point, the feature set is confirmed and slightly richer than stated: transport bar and timeline ruler including markers and arranger sections, track Macro Controls, plug-in parameters via Control Link up to 28 parameters, and a Commands page giving access to factory AND user commands and macros. Platform history: iPad July 2015, then Windows and Surface tablets February 2016, Android tablets June 2017. And the key negative holds — no packet format, handshake, port or third-party client for the Studio One DAW side turned up in any search; the only protocol-level reverse engineering is for StudioLive hardware mixers. Incidental corroboration for a neighbouring finding: a third-party listing shows a Studio One Remote Android build numbered 2.0.0.110052, confirming that PreSonus/Fender really do use the four-part build-string style, which makes 8.2.0.114903 plausible in form. The conclusion that this is a dead end for the user stands.
verdicts.corrected_value: The Remote app's Commands page covers factory and user commands and macros (not just 'Commands'), and Control Link reaches up to 28 plug-in parameters — so the exposed surface is even closer to what an integration would want, still with no published protocol.

verdicts.claim: Studio One supports ReWire
verdicts.reason: Correctly refuted, and the one caveat the finding flagged as unverified is now verified. Search extracts quote the PreSonus KB article 'ReWire Discontinuation Notice for Studio One 6' directly: 'At the end of 2020, Reason Studios discontinued development for ReWire. For this reason, Studio One 6 no longer supports ReWire and it is not included in the program.' So the stated reason is confirmed, not merely plausible, and the version boundary is confirmed by the article body rather than only its title — meaning ReWire is absent from 6, 7 and Fender Studio Pro 8. Two additions: the Studio One 6 release notes say ReWire may still be usable in Studio One 5 and earlier but PreSonus cannot guarantee it works as expected since the technology is no longer updated; and ReWire is separately listed among the features unavailable in the native Apple Silicon build, with Rosetta mode as the fallback. PreSonus's Notion documentation independently marks ReWire as 'not available in Studio One 6 or higher'. The finding's practical note is also right on the substance — ReWire carried audio and transport sync, not editing commands, so it would not have served as an automation bridge anyway.
verdicts.corrected_value: The reason is no longer unverified: the KB states Reason Studios discontinued ReWire development at the end of 2020, which is why Studio One 6 dropped it. Also unavailable in the native Apple Silicon build even before 6.

verdicts.claim: Studio One exposes a named-pipe or socket interface for local IPC
verdicts.reason: The refutation holds and the decisive sentence is verbatim: the embedded SpiderMonkey engine means 'Scripts can read and write files but cannot open sockets.' That is precisely why the design is a filesystem mailbox plus a MIDI note as a doorbell, resent every 150 ms with a 5 s timeout and a 20 ms response poll. No documented named pipe, local HTTP server or scripting CLI entry point surfaced in any search, and the only network listener associated with the DAW is the closed UCNET service for the Remote app. Two refinements: (1) the 'no usable timer' limitation is scoped in the README specifically to Studio One 5 — 'Studio One 5 also gives scripts no usable timer' — so it is not asserted for 6/7/8 and may not hold there; the author simply developed against 5.5.2; (2) the mailbox is larger than the three files named, also carrying edit-request.json, edit-result.json, track-edit-request.json and track-edit-result.json for the MCP Edit and MCP Track Edit extensions. The conclusion — any integration will be file-polling plus MIDI triggers, and that is the ceiling — stands, and is independently consistent with tiwadara/StudioOneMcp arriving at the same shape (control-surface MIDI dispatch plus optional OS-level menu automation) without any socket.
verdicts.corrected_value: The 'no usable timer' limitation is stated for Studio One 5 specifically, not for versions 6/7/8. The mailbox has seven files, not three.

verdicts.claim: REAPER offers official scripting (ReaScript) in Lua/Python plus mature community MCP servers
verdicts.reason: Confirmed, via mirrors independent of the blocked reaper.fm: the Cockos-hosted reascripthelp page, X-Raym's ReaScript API documentation, the Ultraschall mirror, and adamtcroft's guide. All of the finding's substantive points check out — scripts in EEL2, Lua or Python; Lua and EEL2 built in; Python requiring a separate install and enabling in preferences, with some UI features unavailable from Python; and a first-party generated reference that REAPER itself can regenerate from Help > ReaScript documentation, which the sources note is the most reliable copy since the API is extended frequently. One of the named MCP servers is independently verified: xdarkzx-reaper-mcp is live on PyPI at version 0.8.3, 'MCP server for AI-driven music production in REAPER via file-based IPC with a Lua bridge', requires_python >=3.10, Apache-2.0, targeting REAPER 7+ — matching the finding's description of the architecture. Corrections: the generated reference pages I could reach show version 7.83, not 'v7.35' as the finding states, so that figure is stale; and the '2,282 functions' count attributed to reaper-dev-mcp, plus the tool counts for total-reaper-mcp and bonfire-audio/reaper-mcp, are not independently verifiable here because api.github.com is gated for those repos in this session. None of that disturbs the comparison the finding draws, which is the point that matters: REAPER's bridge sits on a documented first-party API, Studio One's on a reverse-engineered one.
verdicts.corrected_value: The generated ReaScript reference is at v7.83, not v7.35. The 2,282-function figure and the per-server tool counts are not independently verifiable here.

verdicts.claim: Ableton Live offers the Live Object Model plus community MCP servers (AbletonMCP)
verdicts.reason: The headline claim is true, but two load-bearing mechanism details are wrong, and mechanism claims are exactly what this pass was meant to catch. (1) The finding says 'The original is ahujasid/ableton-mcp, which drives Live through AbletonOSC, a free Remote Script exposing Live's API over the network.' I read that README directly: it does NOT use AbletonOSC and never mentions it. It installs its own custom MIDI Remote Script described as 'a MIDI Remote Script for Ableton Live that creates a socket server to receive and execute commands', with commands 'sent as JSON objects with a type and optional params', installed via 'uvx --from ableton-mcp ableton-mcp-install-script' into the User Library's Remote Scripts folder, then selected as a Control Surface with Input and Output set to None; prerequisites are Ableton Live 10 or newer, MIT licence. An independent search summary states the same: 'The ahujasid version instead uses its own socket-based Remote Script, not AbletonOSC.' So the finding has the architecture backwards — the JSON-over-TCP socket server it attributes to 'forks [that] took it further' is the original's own design, while the AbletonOSC-based servers are different projects (adindotdev/ableton-mcp, Simon-Kansara/ableton-live-mcp-server). AbletonOSC itself is real — a Remote Script exposing the LOM over OSC, listening on 11000 and replying on 11001, requiring Live 11+. (2) The finding's explanatory punchline, that 'Live ships a documented Python Remote Script layer', is wrong: community LOM references state 'The API is officially undocumented by Ableton — this reference is based on community documentation from Cycling '74's Max for Live LOM reference', and an Ableton forum post from May 2026 circulates unofficial LOM docs for Live 9 to 12. Ableton's real advantage over Studio One is a stable Remote Script extension point with network exposure, not official documentation — both LOMs are reverse-engineered. The finding's conclusion (Ableton is genuinely agent-controllable, not worth switching to) survives, but the reasoning given for it does not.
verdicts.corrected_value: ahujasid/ableton-mcp uses its own socket-based MIDI Remote Script (JSON over TCP), not AbletonOSC; Live 10+; MIT. AbletonOSC-based servers are adindotdev/ableton-mcp and Simon-Kansara/ableton-live-mcp-server (AbletonOSC: Live 11+, ports 11000/11001). The Live Object Model is officially UNDOCUMENTED by Ableton; the nearest reference is Cycling '74's Max for Live LOM docs. The real difference from Studio One is a stable network-exposed Remote Script extension point, not official docs.

verdicts.claim: PreSonus Studio One was rebranded as Fender Studio Pro, with version 8 the first release under the new name
verdicts.reason: Confirmed by multiple independent outlets: MusicTech ('PreSonus Studio One Pro becomes Fender Studio Pro'), Mixdown, Music Connection, Production Expert and Sound On Sound all report the rename taking effect 13 January 2026, with Quantum becoming the Fender Quantum Series and AudioBox becoming Fender AudioBox. Fender's acquisition of PreSonus in 2021 is confirmed, as is Fender taking over licensing, subscriptions and support, with PreSonus account pages now redirecting to My.Fender.com, and the PreSonus brand continuing for hardware. Fender Studio Pro 8 as the successor to Studio One Pro 7 is confirmed by both Mixdown and the Sound On Sound review. The search-visibility point is confirmed verbatim in substance by the SoS review, which notes many other products use 'Studio Pro' and that years of 'Studio One' tutorials are now harder to find — so the finding's practical advice to search 'Studio One' rather than 'Fender Studio Pro' is well grounded, and my own searching bore it out repeatedly. Minor unverified details: the specific month of the acquisition (November 2021) was not pinned down in the extracts I could reach, only the year; and the version 8 feature list (Mustang/Rumble Native, Studio Verb, Arrangement Overview, Chord Assistant) was corroborated in outline rather than item by item. Note also that support.presonus.com still hosts the Fender Studio Pro knowledge base, so the old domain remains the documentation home.
verdicts.corrected_value: Acquisition year 2021 confirmed; the specific month (November) is not independently verified here. Note that Fender Studio Pro support articles still live on support.presonus.com.

verdicts.claim: The downloaded build is Fender Studio Pro 8 version 8.2.0.114903
verdicts.reason: Not independently verifiable as to the exact build string, which is what the finding already concluded. The 8.2 release itself is firmly confirmed: Fender's own newsroom post is dated 20 October 2026, with coverage from ProSoundWeb, Mixonline, Production Expert, rekkerd, gearnews and thatericalper the same week, so a download six days before today being 8.2 is consistent. The feature list checks out independently — Trim Automation (volume change without redrawing existing automation), Dim Solo Mode (dims other channels while already-muted channels stay muted), Multiple Marker Tracks settable by time or bar/beat, extended Stem Separation adding guitar and piano, Vocal Tune Low Latency under 3 ms, Per Note Sound Variations, and MIDI 2.0 with high-resolution velocity and controller data shown in the Note Editor. Free for Pro+ subscribers and qualifying perpetual licence holders is confirmed. The MIDI 2.0 Windows caveat is confirmed and sharper than stated: MIDI 2.0 currently works on macOS and Linux, with Windows pending Microsoft's official release, which needs Windows 11 25H2 or later — directly relevant to this Windows user. The build number 114903 appears in no source I could reach, and Fender's version page and release notes were not retrievable (fender.com and s1toolbox.com are DNS-blocked here). The finding's plausibility argument is now better supported: a Studio One Remote Android build is independently listed as 2.0.0.110052, confirming the four-part style. The authoritative check is the user's own Help > About dialog.
verdicts.corrected_value: 8.2 and its feature set are confirmed (Fender newsroom, 20 October 2026); the build string 8.2.0.114903 is not independently verifiable — confirm in Help > About. MIDI 2.0 currently works on macOS and Linux only; Windows needs Windows 11 25H2+ and Microsoft's release.

verdicts.claim: Fender Studio Pro 8 can convert a recorded performance into editable MIDI natively
verdicts.reason: Confirmed by sources independent of the retailer page cited. Both functions are real and distinct: Extract Notes analyses pitched audio and handles both monophonic and polyphonic material — single-note lines like vocals or bass as well as chords from guitar or piano — producing MIDI on a new Instrument Track that can then be edited or reassigned to any virtual instrument; Extract Beats is the drum-focused counterpart, looking for rhythmic events rather than pitch, with results landing on an Instrument Track usually loaded with Impact. Corroborated by makingascene.org's Fender Studio Pro 8 coverage and a Japanese walkthrough on note.com, which also supplies the menu path the finding lacked: right-click the audio event and choose Extract Notes from the Audio menu. One correction: no independent source mentions Mai Tai. Impact for Extract Beats is corroborated; 'assigned to Mai Tai' for Extract Notes is not, and the better-supported statement is simply that the result lands on a new Instrument Track and can be reassigned to any instrument. The copyright reasoning is sound and is the most important part of this finding for the user: these are deterministic analysis tools that transcribe the user's own performance rather than generating new musical material, so they do not compromise human authorship — unlike the Moises backing-track generation noted in the Studio Assistant finding.
verdicts.corrected_value: Extract Beats → Impact is corroborated; 'Extract Notes → Mai Tai' is not independently verifiable. Menu path: right-click the audio event > Audio > Extract Notes.

verdicts.claim: Fender Studio Pro's built-in 'Studio Assistant' can act as an agent that composes or edits in the DAW
verdicts.reason: Correctly refuted, and independently so. KVR, Mixdown, Mixonline, Major HiFi, geargods and rekkerd all describe Studio Assistant, introduced in 8.1, as an in-DAW natural-language helper that consolidates documentation, tutorials and support into one panel and answers questions without pulling the user out of the session. One review states the point explicitly: Studio Assistant is 'guidance, not a full AI engineer taking over the session'. Nothing in any coverage describes it editing MIDI, creating tracks or executing commands, which is what the claim asserts. Public-beta-for-Pro+ is confirmed across outlets. Added detail: Mixonline dates the 8.1 release to 10 June 2026. The Moises integration is confirmed as part of 8.1 alongside a native Vocal Tune plug-in, and the finding's distinction is the right one — stem separation and vocal tuning applied to the user's own recording are analysis/processing, whereas Moises backing-track generation is generative and is the feature to avoid for clean sole authorship. Not independently verified: the specific Moises free-tier quotas (10 stem separations, 120 stem generations, 5 voice conversions per month), and any pricing or accuracy claims beyond Pro+ availability. No official Fender help-centre page or release notes for the assistant were reachable from this container.
verdicts.corrected_value: 8.1 released 10 June 2026 (Mixonline). The Moises free-tier quotas cited in the finding are not independently verifiable.

verdicts.claim: MIDI files can be exchanged reliably between Studio One and an external assistant
verdicts.reason: Confirmed, and the key facts are corroborated by a second official KB article distinct from the one cited — the general 'Studio One: MIDI FAQ' (support.presonus.com/hc/en-us/articles/360004944692), plus a dedicated 'Studio One: Export MIDI Tracks' article. PreSonus recommends File > Save As and selecting .mid or .midi when you need the tempo map and song markers included, and states that other export methods do not capture all of that data — so the finding's advice to prefer Save As is vendor-backed. The Type 1 restriction is also stated in PreSonus's own KB: Studio One exports Type 1 (multitrack) MIDI only, not Type 0. The drag-out limitation is independently corroborated by a different source than the Toontrack thread cited: a PreSonus answers.presonus.com thread ('Need to drag one track out of studio 1 and into explorer in wav format') confirms you cannot drag to export directly to Windows Explorer, with the Browser's Files tab as the workaround. Two refinements: (1) 'Type 1 only' is not absolute — a 2015 third-party walkthrough reports that selecting tracks, right-clicking and choosing 'Export Parts to MIDI File' produces a Type 0 file, so a Type 0 route may exist via a different command, though this is unverified on current versions; (2) a separate Windows issue exists in the opposite direction — if Studio One runs as administrator, Explorer cannot drop files into it, and PreSonus's KB fix is to untick 'run this program as administrator' on Studio One.exe. Both of those are worth knowing, and neither undermines the working loop the finding describes, which remains the one approach that needs no setup.
verdicts.corrected_value: 'Type 1 only' applies to File > Save As; a right-click 'Export Parts to MIDI File' route is reported to produce Type 0 (unverified on current versions). Also: if Studio One runs as administrator, dragging files INTO it from Explorer fails — untick 'run as administrator' on Studio One.exe.

findings.claim: A mature, MIDI-focused MCP server exists that an AI can use to read and edit a user's MIDI files
findings.detail: As of 2026-10-26 no MIDI MCP server has meaningful adoption or a maintained read+edit feature set. The official MCP registry (registry.modelcontextprotocol.io) returns only TWO results for search=midi, and neither composes: io.github.mrfentmen/midi-tools-mcp v1.0.0 (npm 'midi-tools-mcp', described as 'MIDI note math: note names, frequencies, and note numbers. No network and no key.') and an unrelated web-scraping server. search=studio-one returns 0 results. Every candidate found on GitHub is a solo hobby project in the 0-57 star range.
findings.practical: Do not build your workflow around a MIDI MCP server. None is reliable enough. Use the music21 path below instead.

findings.claim: music21 lets the assistant read your MIDI, change instruments, and add bass/drum tracks with no MCP server at all
findings.detail: music21 10.5.1, BSD-3-Clause, uploaded to PyPI 2026-10-22 (four days before today), requires_python >=3.11, maintained by cuthbertLab (MIT academic project). I installed it in this container and ran a full round trip: wrote a 6-note piano MIDI, re-parsed it, swapped the instrument to Violin, derived a bass part at -24 semitones, added a percussion part, and wrote it back out. Verified the output with mido: 4 tracks, Violin = GM program 40 on channel 0, Electric Bass = GM program 33 on channel 1, Bass Drum correctly routed to channel 9 (= MIDI channel 10, the GM percussion channel). Working scripts are at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user--/4b2bd38e-8d7f-52a5-bb39-0e1615b1f404/scratchpad/t3.py with output /tmp/claude-0/-home-user--/4b2bd38e-8d7f-52a5-bb39-0e1615b1f404/scratchpad/out.mid. One real gotcha I hit: a Part built note-by-note and inserted into a parsed Score raises 'StreamException: cannot process repeats on Stream that does not contain measures' on write('midi') — you must call .makeMeasures() on each newly built Part first. Also note converter.parse() on a plain MIDI file returns instrument None, so instrument identity must be set explicitly rather than read back.
findings.practical: This is your path. Export MIDI from Fender Studio Pro 8, attach the .mid file to the chat, and the assistant edits it with music21 and hands back a .mid you re-import. Setup time for you: zero — it runs in the assistant's container, not on your PC. Because every change is a deterministic rule you asked for (transpose, reassign GM program, duplicate rhythm), it is editing your notes, not generating music.

findings.claim: An MCP server exists for PreSonus Studio One that can read .song files and drive a running instance
findings.detail: studio-one-mcp is real: npm package 'studio-one-mcp' v0.3.0, MIT, published 2026-09-30, upstream repo NeanderthalMan/studio-one-mcp (12 stars, 2 forks, 72 commits, status explicitly 'early'). A fork S-kkipie/studio-one-mcp (0 stars, 187 commits) was tested on Windows 11 with Studio One 7.2.3. Install is 'npx -y studio-one-mcp setup'. It exposes ~1,400 commands (1,429 on Studio One 7): song reading/diffing, transport, tracks, markers, mixer, plug-ins, arranger sections, tempo, note editing, chord/drum writing, bounce/import/export. The song_* tools parse .song zip/XML directly with Studio One closed. BUT: upstream was developed against Studio One 5.5.2 on macOS, and 'Studio One 6/7 and Studio Pro 8 are wired in but untested'. On Windows the live bridge needs the third-party loopMIDI driver with a port named 'studio-one-mcp', plus a 'MCP Bridge' control-surface script installed into your user profile and then added by hand in Studio One under External Devices (Receive From = the virtual port, Send To = None), communicating via a file mailbox with a MIDI note as doorbell. Documented caveats: plug-in changes are read-modify-write and can overwrite edits made in the plug-in window, undo behaves unexpectedly after some mixer changes, a live change feed was abandoned because it crashed Studio One three times, and anything running as your user can control Studio One through the mailbox folder.
findings.practical: Not a 30-minute non-programmer setup, and your Pro 8 is the specific version the author flags as untested. Skip the live bridge. If you ever do try it, use only the song_* read tools on a COPY of your .song file, never the live/plug-in tools on a project you care about.

findings.claim: Studio One / Fender Studio Pro 8 has a public scripting API an MCP server could use properly
findings.detail: The studio-one-mcp README states plainly: 'Studio One has no public API, no OSC, and no network scripting' — which is why that project resorts to a control-surface script plus a file mailbox. A community-maintained reference exists at CSources/Studio-Pro-Scripting-API-Reference (covering CCL.JS, Engine.JS, Host API) but its own description says 'NOT OFFICIAL, these are community-maintained references. It's incomplete and potentially incorrect.' Community reports add that the scripting API can set a plug-in parameter by name only for PreSonus plug-ins and cannot enumerate any plug-in's parameters, and that automation editing is not exposed.
findings.practical: There is no clean, supported way to wire an AI directly into Studio One 6, 7, or Pro 8. Treat MIDI file export/import as the interface — it is stable, documented, and version-independent across all three of your installs.

findings.claim: The official filesystem MCP server would let this cloud assistant read a folder on the user's Windows PC
findings.detail: @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem is real and very actively maintained — v2.0.1 published 2026-10-25 (one day before today), 22 versions since 2024-11-21, MIT, install 'npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem <allowed-dir> ...', requires Node.js 24+, and it does read/write/list/tree/search/move within the directories passed as arguments. But its transport is stdio, meaning it runs as a child process of the MCP client on the SAME machine. Every filesystem server in the official registry is likewise transport 'stdio' (checked: Digital-Defiance/mcp-filesystem, bytedance/mcp-server-filesystem, domdomegg/filesystem-mcp, Oncorporation/filesystem-server, fieldcure/filesystem); the only non-stdio one, pulsemcp/remote-filesystem, reads Google Cloud Storage buckets, not your PC. There is no MCP server that exposes a Windows disk to a cloud container. Confirmed from the other direction by this session's own environment documentation: 'This session runs in a cloud container and cannot reach their computer.'
findings.practical: Installing a filesystem MCP server on your PC will not make a cloud chat see your Studio One folder. Either attach the .mid file to the chat (simplest), or run the assistant locally so it already has your disk.

findings.claim: Claude's own local-session / Remote Control feature is the realistic way to give the assistant direct access to a Windows project folder
findings.detail: Per the official Claude Code desktop docs: Windows is supported natively (x64 installer plus a separate ARM64 installer). A LOCAL session 'runs on your machine with direct access to your files', and you pick the working folder via 'the project folder control next to the environment selector'. Cloud sessions instead make you select repositories and run on Anthropic-managed infrastructure. Remote Control then makes a local session reachable from your other devices — toggled per-session by its Remote Control switch or by typing '/remote-control' in the prompt box; it can be disabled globally by setting 'disableRemoteControl' to true in ~/.claude/settings.json. This session's environment docs give the CLI equivalent: run 'claude remote-control' in a terminal in the folder you want to work in, which then appears in the Claude Code app.
findings.practical: Install the Claude Code desktop app on your Windows PC, start a LOCAL session, and point the project folder at your Studio One export folder (e.g. C:\Users\<you>\Documents\Studio One\Songs\MyTrack). The assistant then reads and writes your .mid files in place with no MCP server, no loopMIDI, and no bridge. This is the under-30-minutes option.

findings.claim: tubone24/midi-mcp-server is a usable MIDI MCP server
findings.detail: It is the most-starred and most-alive option: 57 stars, 11 forks, MIT, 39 commits, most recent commit Apr 12, 2026 (commit-date headers run Apr 12 2026, Apr 11 2026, Mar 31 2026, Dec 21 2025, Nov 17 2025, May 7 2025...). Install: 'npm install' then 'npm run build', run as 'node build/index.js' (stdio) or 'node build/index.js --http [--port=8080]'. But it exposes only TWO tools — create_midi (build a MIDI file from structured JSON, with a preview UI) and parse_chord (chord name to MIDI pitches) — and the docs describe creating new files only, never loading or editing an existing one. It lists @tonejs/midi solely for the preview UI. A hosted endpoint 'https://midi-mcp-server.tubone24.workers.dev/mcp' is documented but I could NOT verify it: this container's proxy refused the CONNECT tunnel with 403, so treat its availability as unconfirmed.
findings.practical: Useless for your actual need, which is editing MIDI you played yourself. It can only emit new MIDI from JSON — closer to the AI-generation you want to avoid. Skip it.

findings.claim: xiaolaa2/midi-file-mcp can read and modify existing MIDI files including instruments
findings.detail: 11 stars, 3 forks, MIT. Install 'npx -y midi-file-mcp'. Built on Tone.js/@tonejs/midi. It genuinely reads: get_midi_info, get_tracks_info, get_track_info_by_index, get_notes_by_index, get_pitchbends_by_index, get_controlchanges_by_index. Its write side is ADD-only: set_tempo, add_notes_by_index, add_controlchanges_by_index, add_pitchbends_by_index, add_track — no tool edits or deletes existing events, and crucially there is NO program-change / instrument-assignment tool, so it cannot do the piano-to-violin swap you asked for. It is also stale: npm 'midi-file-mcp' latest is 0.1.3 with the last publish on 2025-04-02, about 19 months before today, across only 4 versions.
findings.practical: Cannot change an instrument, which is your main request. Not worth installing.

findings.claim: brightlikethelight/music21-mcp-server wraps music21 as an MCP server you can pip install
