findings.detail: The repo is the most feature-complete music21 MCP wrapper on paper: 28 stars, 9 forks, MIT, 196 commits, 13 tools (import_score, list_scores, get_score_info, export_score, delete_score, analyze_key, analyze_chords, analyze_harmony, analyze_voice_leading, recognize_patterns, harmonize_melody, generate_counterpoint, imitate_style) with MIDI import/export claimed. But its documented install command does not work: 'pip install music21-mcp-server' fails because the package is NOT on PyPI — https://pypi.org/pypi/music21-mcp-server/json returns HTTP 404 {"message": "Not Found"}. Its own README also self-reports MCP interface reliability at just 40-50% (versus 95%+ HTTP, 99%+ CLI/Python), and contradicts itself on Docker/Kubernetes/auth support between the README and the About text.
findings.practical: Ignore the MCP wrapper and its broken install. You get the same music21 power, at 99% reliability by the author's own numbers, by having the assistant call the music21 library directly — which is exactly what I verified working above.

findings.claim: sandst1/mcp-server-midi can send MIDI notes live into a DAW on Windows
findings.detail: The server is real (17 stars, 5 forks, MIT, but only 3 commits; Python 3.7+, FastMCP over SSE at http://localhost:8123/sse, tools for Note On, Note Off, Control Change, and timed MIDI Sequence) and it works by creating a virtual MIDI output port named 'MCP MIDI Out' via rtmidi. That approach cannot work on Windows: upstream RtMidi documents virtual ports for 'The Linux ALSA, Macintosh CoreMIDI and JACK APIs' only, and python-rtmidi raises 'UnsupportedOperationError: Virtual ports not supported (Windows MM)'. Mido's RtMidi backend docs say the same and name Tobias Erichsen's loopMIDI as the workaround. The repo lists no OS requirement and uses a Unix-style 'source .venv/bin/activate'. Variants klaborda/mcp-server-midi and jppassalacqua/midi-mcp-server are forks of this and tubone24 respectively, not independent options.
findings.practical: Would need you to install loopMIDI and patch the code before it ran at all on Windows. And live note-streaming is the wrong shape for your goal anyway — you want to keep authorship, which means editing files you played, not having an AI play notes into your DAW.

findings.claim: A free, no-auth MCP server exists for music notation, harmonic analysis and MIDI rendering
findings.detail: Gradus Notation: npm '@gradusmusic/notation-mcp' v0.8.0, MIT, created 2026-05-07 and last modified 2026-08-26, repo delmas41/gradusnotation (only 3 stars). Install: 'claude mcp add gradus-notation -- npx -y @gradusmusic/notation-mcp'. No API key, explicitly 'no auth'. 20 tools including notation_render (JSON score to SVG + MusicXML + MIDI in one call), theory_analyze_score (Roman numerals, keys, modulations, cadences, texture), counterpoint_check, voice_leading_patterns and engraving_check against a citable rulebook (rule text and figured-bass corpus are CC BY 4.0). It is stdio-only — no hosted MCP endpoint; the GRADUS_NOTATION_API_BASE env var (default https://gradusmusic.com) points at its REST backend, not an MCP URL. It is also registered in the official MCP registry as com.gradusmusic/notation.
findings.practical: Genuinely a sub-10-minute install if you want engraved sheet-music PDFs/SVGs and Roman-numeral analysis of your own arrangement. It renders scores from notation data — it will not open and edit the .mid file you exported, so it complements the music21 path rather than replacing it.

findings.claim: TripleAt/midi-mcp is a safe open-source option for opening and editing MIDI by path
findings.detail: Functionally it is the closest match to the need — tools open_midi, get_tracks, insert_notes, insert_events, commit, save_as, quantize, with documented transpose/quantize/humanize transformations, installed via 'npm install' + 'npm run build' + 'node dist/index.js'. But it has 0 stars, 0 forks, and no licence: the README itself says the repo 'does not include a license file' and that without explicit permission it should be treated as 'All rights reserved.' No instrument-change capability is mentioned.
findings.practical: Avoid. With no licence grant you have no right to use or redistribute it, which is exactly the wrong footing for a project where you care about owning the copyright in the output.

findings.claim: The npm package named 'midi-mcp' is the canonical MIDI MCP server
findings.detail: npm 'midi-mcp' (repo jazz-soft/midi-mcp) is an unfinished placeholder: latest version 0.0.2, description literally 'coming soon...', only 3 versions, created 2026-04-13 and last modified 2026-05-21. The adjacent name 'mcp-midi' is not registered on npm at all (registry returns 'Not found').
findings.practical: Nothing to install here. If you see 'midi-mcp' recommended somewhere, it is an empty package.

findings.claim: MCP servers for other DAWs are more capable than the Studio One one, so switching DAW is an option
findings.detail: Search surfaced DAW-control MCP servers with large claimed tool counts — MuffinSmith/reaper-mcp (claims 176 tools, body text says 177), bonfire-systems/reaper-mcp (61 tools), Aavishkar-Kolte/reaper-daw-mcp-server, raibid-entertainment/ardour-mcp (claims 111 tools), ptaczek/daw-mcp (Bitwig via Java extension, Ableton via Python Remote Script), WeModulate/bitwig-mcp-server (author-labelled work in progress). REAPER has the richest support because of its public ReaScript API; FL Studio has no dedicated MCP server. I did NOT open these repositories, so star counts, licences, last-commit dates and every feature claim here are unverified, and the ranking of REAPER over Ableton/Bitwig/Cubase comes from a single third-party blog post.
findings.practical: Not a reason to abandon Fender Studio Pro 8. You already own and know it, and the MIDI-file workflow gives you AI help without needing any DAW integration. I would not change DAW on the strength of unverified README claims.

research.recommendation:
Headline: for this user, the answer is to use NO MIDI MCP server at all. The whole category is immature — the official MCP registry returns exactly two hits for "midi" and neither composes, and every GitHub candidate is a 0-57 star solo project. The three that look closest to the need each fail on a hard fact: xiaolaa2/midi-file-mcp has no instrument-change tool and has not shipped since 2025-04-02; brightlikethelight/music21-mcp-server's documented `pip install music21-mcp-server` 404s on PyPI and its README self-reports 40-50% MCP reliability; TripleAt/midi-mcp has no licence file (effectively all rights reserved), which is the wrong footing for a copyright-sensitive project.

What I verified working instead: music21 (10.5.1, BSD-3-Clause, published 2026-10-22). I installed it here and ran the user's exact scenario — parsed a piano MIDI, swapped the part to Violin, derived a bass line at -24 semitones, added a percussion part, wrote it back, then confirmed with mido that the output carried GM program 40 (violin) on ch 0, program 33 (electric bass) on ch 1, and the drum correctly on channel 9 (MIDI ch 10). Scripts and output: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user--/4b2bd38e-8d7f-52a5-bb39-0e1615b1f404/scratchpad/t3.py and /tmp/claude-0/-home-user--/4b2bd38e-8d7f-52a5-bb39-0e1615b1f404/scratchpad/out.mid. One gotcha to carry into the real workflow: any Part built note-by-note needs `.makeMeasures()` before `write('midi')`, or music21 raises "cannot process repeats on Stream that does not contain measures"; and `converter.parse()` on a bare .mid returns instrument None, so instruments must be set explicitly, never read back.

On the file-access question, correct a likely misconception: no filesystem MCP server bridges a cloud container to a Windows disk. @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem is excellent and current (v2.0.1, published 2026-10-25) but is stdio — it runs beside the client on the same machine. Every filesystem server in the registry is stdio except pulsemcp/remote-filesystem, which reads GCS buckets. The actual bridge is Claude's own local session: install the Claude Code desktop app on Windows (natively supported), start a LOCAL session, and set the project folder to the Studio One export directory. That is the only under-30-minutes option that gives direct folder access, and it needs no MCP server, no loopMIDI, and no code.

On Studio One specifically: studio-one-mcp is real and surprisingly ambitious (npm v0.3.0, 2026-09-30, MIT, ~1,429 commands, reads .song files with the DAW closed), but it is self-described as "early", was built against Studio One 5.5.2 on macOS, and explicitly flags "Studio One 6/7 and Studio Pro 8 wired in but untested" — Pro 8 is precisely what this user runs. Its Windows live bridge needs loopMIDI plus a hand-added External Devices control surface and a file-mailbox IPC, and its own docs admit plug-in writes can clobber edits, undo misbehaves, and a change feed crashed Studio One three times. Recommend against the live bridge; the root cause is that Studio One has no public API, no OSC and no network scripting, and the only scripting reference is community-maintained and self-described as incomplete and possibly incorrect.

Recommended setup, in order: (1) Claude Code desktop on Windows, local session pointed at the song folder — or simply attach the .mid to the chat if even that feels like too much; (2) the assistant edits with music21 using deterministic, user-specified transforms; (3) optionally add Gradus Notation (`claude mcp add gradus-notation -- npx -y @gradusmusic/notation-mcp`, MIT, free, no API key) if engraved sheet music and Roman-numeral analysis of the finished arrangement are wanted. Note for the authorship concern this user cares about: the music21 route performs only rule-based edits to notes the user played — transposition, GM program reassignment, rhythmic duplication — which is a materially different provenance story from generative MIDI tools like tubone24's create_midi. Worth stating plainly to the user, while being clear that this is a description of how the tools work and not legal advice on copyright registration.

verdicts.reason: The claim holds and most of the detail is verbatim-accurate. Upstream README confirms 12 stars, 2 forks, 72 commits, MIT, 'Status: early', 'Paths for Windows and for Studio One 6/7 and Studio Pro 8 are wired in but untested', the loopMIDI port named studio-one-mcp, 'External Devices → Add… → studio-one-mcp → MCP Bridge' with Receive From = virtual port and Send To = None, the file mailbox, the undo trap, 'it crashed Studio One three times', and the security note that anything running as your user can drive Studio One through the mailbox. npm studio-one-mcp is v0.3.0, MIT, published 2026-09-30T11:20Z; install is 'npx -y studio-one-mcp setup'. song_* tools do parse .song files with Studio One closed. The fork is confirmed as 0 stars, 0 forks, 187 commits, 'forked from NeanderthalMan/studio-one-mcp', 'tested on Windows 11 with Studio One 7.2.3'.
verdicts.corrected_value: Two corrections, both from conflating the fork with the upstream repo the finding cites as its source. (1) Command count: upstream README says live_command runs 'roughly 1,000 Studio One commands'; the '~1,400 (1,429 on Studio One 7)' figure appears only in the fork's README, and even the fork's own GitHub description still says '~1,000'. Those are Studio One menu commands reachable through one tool, not MCP tools — upstream's table lists ~48 rows / 57 distinct live_*/song_* names. (2) Capability list: 'chord/drum writing' and 'import/export' are fork-only. Upstream has no chord or drum tool, its live_notes is explicitly 'Read-only' (live_edit_notes transposes/quantizes existing notes), and it offers only live_bounce — live_write_chords, live_write_drums, live_create_part, live_write_notes, live_set_chords, live_extract_chords, live_import_audio and live_export are all S-kkipie additions. Also worth knowing: upstream credits Alari81/studio-control with having 'proved the file-mailbox device pattern on Studio Pro 8', so the pattern itself is not untried on Pro 8.

verdicts.claim: Studio One / Fender Studio Pro 8 has a public scripting API an MCP server could use properly
verdicts.reason: Refutation holds, with stronger sourcing than the finding gives. studio-one-mcp's README states verbatim 'Studio One has no public API, no OSC, and no network scripting'. The CSources repo's description reads verbatim 'NOT OFFICIAL, these are community-maintained references.' and 'It's incomplete and potentially incorrect.', and its README adds 'Fender/PreSonus does not provide official public documentation for this API' and 'This reference is entirely community-derived and incomplete'; it has 7 stars and 21 commits and documents Host API, CCL.JS, Engine.JS, Devices.JS, HostUtils, Context, Objects and Skin XML. The automation limit is confirmed by a primary source: 'There is no scripted way to add automation envelope points, so live_write_automation records them the way a person would, in Write mode.'
verdicts.corrected_value: The plug-in-parameter statements are mis-sourced and slightly mis-stated. They are not 'community reports' and are not in the CSources repo given as source_url (that page says nothing about plug-in parameters); they come from studio-one-mcp's README: 'Studio One cannot list a plug-in's parameters, so names come from its presets and Studio One's remote-control map, which covers the PreSonus plug-ins. For other plug-ins, pass the names.' So enumeration is genuinely impossible, but setting a third-party plug-in parameter by name does work if you supply the name yourself. The fork goes further still, reaching third-party plug-in state by driving the plug-in's own Export/Load Preset dialogs — outside the scripting API, read-modify-write, and explicitly not revertible with live_undo.

verdicts.claim: The official filesystem MCP server would let this cloud assistant read a folder on the user's Windows PC
verdicts.reason: Holds. npm metadata confirms @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem 2.0.1 published 2026-10-25T00:05Z, 22 versions, created 2024-11-21T19:14Z, engines node >=24, bin mcp-server-filesystem. Its README confirms the transport in so many words: 'Serves both protocol eras on stdio', and the allow-list is 'Directory access control from command-line arguments'. Stdio means a child process of the client on the same machine, so it cannot bridge a cloud container to a Windows disk. The other direction is confirmed verbatim from this session's own environment documentation: 'This session runs in a cloud container and cannot reach their computer.'
verdicts.corrected_value: Two small things. package.json declares license as 'SEE LICENSE IN LICENSE' rather than the bare 'MIT' quoted (the repo's LICENSE is MIT, so the substance is fine). And I did not re-open each of the five other filesystem servers named, so the sweeping 'every filesystem server in the official registry is likewise transport stdio' is not something I independently reconfirmed — though every npm/PyPI-packaged registry entry I inspected did carry transport stdio.

verdicts.claim: Claude's own local-session / Remote Control feature is the realistic way to give the assistant direct access to a Windows project folder
verdicts.reason: Confirmed verbatim from code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop: 'Download for Windows' / 'For x64 processors' and 'For Windows ARM64, download the ARM64 installer.'; 'Local: runs on your machine with direct access to your files'; 'Project folder: click the project folder control, next to the environment selector, to choose the folder Claude works in.'; 'Cloud: runs on Anthropic-managed infrastructure by default' with repositories selected instead of a folder; Remote Control turned on 'with the session's Remote Control switch, or by typing /remote-control in its prompt box'; and disableRemoteControl set to true in ~/.claude/settings.json to stop sessions connecting. The CLI equivalent is confirmed from this session's environment docs: 'claude remote-control' in a terminal in the folder to work in, which then shows up in the Claude Code app.
verdicts.corrected_value: One omission: the docs also describe automatic connection — 'new sessions connect automatically while Connect new sessions to Remote Control is on in Settings > Claude Code', falling back to remoteControlAtStartup in user or managed settings. So Remote Control is not purely per-session opt-in as the finding implies.

verdicts.claim: tubone24/midi-mcp-server is a usable MIDI MCP server
verdicts.reason: Holds in full. Repo confirms 57 stars, 11 forks, 39 commits, MIT. The commits page lists exactly the dates claimed, newest first: Apr 12 2026, Apr 11 2026, Mar 31 2026, Dec 21 2025, Nov 17 2025, May 7 2025 (then May 5 2025, Apr 7 2025). Only two tools exist — create_midi (structured JSON in, base64 MIDI plus piano-roll preview out) and parse_chord (chord name to MIDI pitches) — and no tool can load, read, parse or edit an existing MIDI file; @tonejs/midi is listed only as a dependency for the preview UI. Install is 'npm install' then 'npm run build', run with node build/index.js or --http [--port=8080]. The hosted endpoint https://midi-mcp-server.tubone24.workers.dev/mcp is documented, and I independently could not reach it either: both a POST tools/list and a plain GET failed with 'CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403' from this container's egress proxy, so 'unconfirmed' is the right label.

verdicts.claim: xiaolaa2/midi-file-mcp can read and modify existing MIDI files including instruments
verdicts.reason: Holds on the decisive point. Repo confirms 11 stars, 3 forks, MIT (17 commits). The tool list is exactly the 11 named: get_midi_info, set_tempo, get_tracks_info, get_track_info_by_index, get_notes_by_index, get_pitchbends_by_index, get_controlchanges_by_index, add_notes_by_index, add_controlchanges_by_index, add_pitchbends_by_index, add_track. There is no program-change / instrument-assignment tool and the page never mentions program change at all, so it cannot do the piano-to-violin swap. Writes are add-only apart from set_tempo. Staleness confirmed: npm midi-file-mcp latest 0.1.3, published 2025-04-02T12:28Z, 4 versions, created the same day.
verdicts.corrected_value: The install command is misquoted: the README documents the Smithery route, 'npx -y @smithery/cli install @xiaolaa2/midi-file-mcp --client claude', not 'npx -y midi-file-mcp' (the npm package does exist, so that invocation may work, but it is not what the project documents). Also worth adding: the README contradicts itself, claiming in its feature list that it can 'modify' note, control-change and pitch-bend information while its own operations table shows only add and get.

verdicts.claim: brightlikethelight/music21-mcp-server wraps music21 as an MCP server you can pip install
verdicts.reason: Refutation holds. https://pypi.org/pypi/music21-mcp-server/json returns HTTP 404 with body {"message": "Not Found"}, while the README's documented install is verbatim 'pip install music21-mcp-server' — so the documented install cannot work. Repo confirms 28 stars, 9 forks, MIT, 196 commits and exactly the 13 tools listed. The self-reported reliability table confirms MCP 40-50%, HTTP 95%+, CLI 99%+, Python 99%+. The Docker/Kubernetes/auth contradiction is real: the About text advertises 'FastMCP • music21 • OAuth2 • Docker' with docker/kubernetes/oauth2 topics, while the README's migration section says Docker, K8s, complex auth and monitoring were removed as 'too unstable for MCP ecosystem' — and Dockerfile and docker-compose.yml are still in the tree.
verdicts.corrected_value: Minor addition: the reliability numbers are internally inconsistent too — the design section separately states the server 'Works even when MCP fails (30-40% of time)', which does not square with a 40-50% MCP success rate. Treat all four percentages as the author's unsourced self-assessment, not measurements.

verdicts.claim: sandst1/mcp-server-midi can send MIDI notes live into a DAW on Windows
verdicts.reason: Refutation holds on three independent primary sources. The repo confirms 17 stars, 5 forks, 3 commits, MIT, Python 3.7+, FastMCP over SSE at http://localhost:8123/sse, four operations (Note On, Note Off, Control Change, MIDI Sequence), 'The server creates a virtual MIDI port named "MCP MIDI Out"', rtmidi as a requirement, no OS statement anywhere, and the Unix-only 'source .venv/bin/activate'. RtMidi's own header (RtMidi.h, master) says openVirtualPort 'is currently only supported by the CoreMIDI (macOS and iOS), ALSA and JACK APIs (the other APIs report a warning and open nothing)', and its tutorial says 'The Linux ALSA, Macintosh CoreMIDI and JACK APIs allow for the establishment of virtual input and output MIDI ports'. Mido's RtMidi backend doc states 'Virtual Ports are **not** available under Microsoft Windows. An alternative is to use third party software such as Tobias Erichsen's loopMIDI'.
verdicts.corrected_value: The quoted Python error is wrong. I downloaded the python-rtmidi 1.5.8 sdist and read src/_rtmidi.pyx: open_virtual_port raises NotImplementedError('Virtual ports are not supported by the Windows MultiMedia API.') — the docstring promises UnsupportedOperationError but the code does not raise it, and the string 'Virtual ports not supported (Windows MM)' appears nowhere. Also, for completeness: RtMidi 6.1.0 added a Windows MIDI Services backend (opt-in, Windows 11 25H2+), but its virtual-port documentation still lists only CoreMIDI/ALSA/JACK, so the conclusion is correct as of today.

verdicts.claim: A free, no-auth MCP server exists for music notation, harmonic analysis and MIDI rendering
verdicts.reason: Confirmed on both sources. npm @gradusmusic/notation-mcp is v0.8.0, MIT, created 2026-05-07T03:20Z, latest published 2026-08-26T04:02Z, repo delmas41/gradusnotation. That repo has 3 stars, 0 forks, MIT, documents exactly 20 tools in six groups (notation_render, notation_validate, knowledge_search, notation_examples, notation_schema; theory_analyze_score, theory_parse_xml, theory_validate_ranges, theory_respell, theory_pitch_utils; engraving_rules, engraving_rule, engraving_check; music_critique, counterpoint_check, corpus_search; voice_leading_patterns, voice_leading_pattern; figured_bass_exercises, figured_bass_exercise), gives the install command 'claude mcp add gradus-notation -- npx -y @gradusmusic/notation-mcp', states 'Free to use, no auth, no API key', describes GRADUS_NOTATION_API_BASE (default https://gradusmusic.com) as an 'Override for self-hosted or local-dev API' with no remote MCP endpoint listed, renders 'JSON score → SVG + MusicXML + MIDI in one call', puts rule text and the figured-bass corpus under CC BY 4.0, and is in the official registry as com.gradusmusic/notation with versions through 0.8.0. It cannot open or edit an existing .mid.
verdicts.corrected_value: One practical sharpening: the tools that read a file take MusicXML, not MIDI (engraving_check accepts a local MusicXML path, theory_analyze_score parses MusicXML). So to analyse or engrave the arrangement you played, the .mid has to be converted to MusicXML first — which music21 does in one line, making the two paths complementary exactly as the finding says.

verdicts.claim: TripleAt/midi-mcp is a safe open-source option for opening and editing MIDI by path
verdicts.reason: Refutation holds and is if anything understated. The repo has 0 stars and 0 forks (44 commits on master), the tools are as described (open_midi, get_tracks, insert_notes, insert_events, quantize, commit, save_as, plus unnamed transpose/humanize/scale-constrain transformations), insert_events covers only note, CC and pitch-bend events, and no instrument/program-change capability is documented. The README's licence section reads verbatim: 'This repository does not include a license file (without explicit permission, it should be treated as effectively All rights reserved).'
verdicts.corrected_value: A LICENSE.md file does exist on master, which superficially contradicts 'does not include a license file' — but reading it confirms the conclusion rather than undermining it. In full it says: 'This repository does not include a standalone license for the project itself. Please refer to the licenses of the bundled dependencies and libraries used by this project, and comply with their terms when using or redistributing this code. If you plan to publish or redistribute this repository, you are responsible for confirming and honoring the applicable third-party licenses.' That is a disclaimer, not a grant, so there is still no permission to use or redistribute the project's own code.

verdicts.claim: The npm package named 'midi-mcp' is the canonical MIDI MCP server
verdicts.reason: Refutation holds exactly. https://registry.npmjs.org/midi-mcp gives dist-tags.latest = 0.0.2, description 'coming soon...', three versions (0.0.0, 0.0.1, 0.0.2), created 2026-04-13T00:49Z, modified 2026-05-21T02:55Z, repository git+https://github.com/jazz-soft/midi-mcp.git. https://registry.npmjs.org/mcp-midi returns HTTP 404 with body {"error":"Not found"}. Nothing to install.

verdicts.claim: MCP servers for other DAWs are more capable than the Studio One one, so switching DAW is an option
verdicts.reason: The capability comparison itself is not independently verifiable — no primary source ranks these servers against each other, and the ranking of REAPER over Ableton/Bitwig/Cubase still rests on one third-party blog post. The practical conclusion (do not switch DAW on the strength of README claims) stands. I did verify the specific repo named: MuffinSmith/reaper-mcp is MIT with 46 commits, and the 176-versus-177 contradiction is real — About says '176 tools for mixing, mastering, MIDI composition, and full music production' while the body and badge say 177. Registry searches for 'bitwig' and 'cubase' return 0 results.
verdicts.corrected_value: Two corrections. (1) 'FL Studio has no dedicated MCP server' is false: the official registry lists io.github.origami-research/fl-studio-agent v0.1.1 ('Drive FL Studio from an AI agent: write notes, set tempo and levels, check what sounds, render') and io.github.synopsys0/postfader-fl-studio-mcp v0.10.0 ('Read-back-verified mixer and plug-in control for FL Studio 2026 on macOS, with audio analysis'). (2) The source_url points at a fork, not the project: MuffinSmith/reaper-mcp has 0 stars and 0 forks and is shown as 'forked from TwelveTake-Studios/reaper-mcp', whose upstream is the one in the official registry as com.twelvetake/reaper-mcp v1.7.8. Also missing from the list: io.github.AMEOBIUS/opendaw-mcp (255-261 tools) for the browser-based openDAW, and four Ableton servers in the registry.

findings.claim: Studio One was rebranded by Fender; the product is now "Fender Studio Pro", effective 13 January 2026.
findings.detail: Sound On Sound: "From 13 January 2026, Studio One will now be known as Fender Studio Pro", with Quantum/AudioBox interfaces becoming Fender Quantum Series / Fender AudioBox, and MyPreSonus accounts moving to MyFender. The PreSonus name stays on Eris monitors, StudioLive mixers and Air loudspeakers. Fender acquired PreSonus in 2021. The official manual now lives at fenderstudiopromanual.fender.com (the older Studio One 6/7 manual is still at s1manual.presonus.com), and the in-app path is Help > Studio Pro Reference Manual.
findings.practical: Treat "Fender Studio Pro 8" and "Studio One Pro 8" as the same program. Your v6 and v7 installs keep their old names and menus, so steps below note where wording differs.

findings.claim: The installed version is Fender Studio Pro Pro 8, build 8.2.0.114903.
findings.detail: That 8.2 exists is confirmed: Fender's newsroom press release for "Fender Studio Pro 8.2" is dated 20 October 2026 and lists Trim Automation, Dim Solo Mode, Multiple Marker Tracks, Vocal Tune Follow + Low Latency, stem separation extended to guitar and piano, Per Note Sound Variations, Plug-in Replacement from the context menu, and MIDI 2.0. I could not find any primary source publishing the four-part build string 8.2.0.114903, so the exact build cannot be confirmed (Wikipedia's infobox still shows 8.0.2 and is stale). Note Fender states MIDI 2.0 on Windows needs Windows 11 25H2 or later.
findings.practical: Read your own build from Help > About rather than trusting a quoted number. Nothing in the MIDI export/import workflow below depends on the exact build.

findings.claim: In version 8, a "Song" is now called a "Session".
findings.detail: Macworld's review states files are saved as "sessions" (formerly "songs"); Bobby Owsinski's blog likewise reports "songs are now called sessions", and that Pro 8 opens all previous PreSonus Studio One songs. The Fender manual's page titles reflect this: "Export Stems from your Session", and the MIDI setup page refers to "exporting the Session". Neither Fender nor the press gives a reason for the rename.
findings.practical: When you read a Studio One 6/7 tutorial that says "Song menu" or "export the Song", look for "Session" in Pro 8. The File menu items you need (Save As…, Convert To…) keep their names.

findings.claim: MIDI is exported with File > Export > MIDI File.
findings.detail: No such menu item is documented. The official manual says: "You can export an entire Song as a .MID file using the Save As… or Convert To… command from the File menu. All tempo information, tracks, and track names will be retained." PreSonus support repeats this: "If you want to export a Standard MIDI File that includes all of the necessary attributes such as tempo map and song markers, use File > Save As... and select *.mid or *.midi as the export format in the export dialog's file format selector box. Some of the other export methods do not capture all of that data." File > Export in Studio One is for media/audio; the Export Stems page lists only audio formats (Wave, AIFF, FLAC, CAF, Ogg Vorbis, M4A, AAC/ALAC, MP3) — there is no MIDI option there.
findings.practical: To send me the whole arrangement: File > Save As… > set the file-type selector to *.mid > name it > Save. Do not look for File > Export; that path will only give you audio.

findings.claim: File > Save As… to .mid exports the whole song (all tracks), not just selected ones, and keeps tempo and track names.
findings.detail: Manual: "You can export an entire Song as a .MID file using the Save As… or Convert To… command from the File menu. All tempo information, tracks, and track names will be retained." A Toontrack forum user independently confirms a Studio One Save As .mid carried the tempo map intact into Superior Drummer 3. Track selection is not mentioned as affecting this export, and nothing in the documentation suggests it does — so "all tracks" is the documented behaviour, while "selection is ignored" is inference, not a quoted fact.
findings.practical: This is the export to use. One file, every track, correct BPM — exactly what my analysis script needs, since it reads the tempo out of the MIDI header (and I otherwise have to be told the BPM by hand with --tempo).

findings.claim: You can export only the parts you select, via right-click > Export Selection.
findings.detail: Manual: "To export an Instrument Part to a MIDI file, [Right]/[Ctrl]-click on the Part and select Export Selection. Choose a file name and storage location in the pop-up window, and choose a file type (Musicloop or Standard MIDI file)." The same page adds: "Multiple Instrument Parts can be exported at once to a single file." The command is "Export Selection" — not "Export as MIDI"; I found no primary source for an "Export as MIDI file" item in any version.
findings.practical: When you only want me to look at the piano you just played: click the part, right-click it, Export Selection, choose Standard MIDI file. Pick Standard MIDI file, not Musicloop — Musicloop is a Studio One-only format.

findings.claim: Dragging a part into the Browser exports it; hold Alt to get a MIDI file instead of a Musicloop.
findings.detail: The drag-export exists and is officially recommended ("drag-and-drop to the Files tab" is called one of the most efficient methods), but the modifier key is inconsistent across sources. The Studio One manual's Browser page says: "As you hover over the Browser, you can press [Alt] to choose between Musicloop and MIDI file formats." A Fender feature-request thread describes the current behaviour as "drag the MIDI clip to a file browser tab, then press the shift key to export as type MIDI instead". A KVR user reports a chooser box appearing with "music loop" and "standard MIDI file" and Alt moving the selection. A separate KVR report says the Musicloop option trims empty space at the start, which makes clips land wrong in other software.
findings.practical: Workable but fiddly: drag, and before releasing watch the pop-up/cursor — try Alt, then Shift if Alt does nothing in your build. Because of the trimming risk and the modifier ambiguity, prefer Save As… (whole session) or right-click > Export Selection (one part). Drag-export is a convenience, not the reliable path.

findings.claim: Studio One writes Type 1 (multitrack) MIDI files only.
findings.detail: PreSonus MIDI FAQ: "Studio One only exports Type 1 (multitrack) MIDI files, not Type 0." The same FAQ also notes "Studio One doesn't capture program changes in it's MIDI file exports" — PreSonus flags that article as possibly out of date, so treat the program-change limitation as likely-but-not-current-verified.
findings.practical: Good news for this workflow: Type 1 keeps your tracks separate, so I can see piano, bass and drums as distinct tracks and name them back to you. The practical consequence of the program-change gap is the next finding.

findings.claim: Instrument assignments survive the MIDI round trip.
findings.detail: A Standard MIDI File carries note data, tempo, track names and (at most) GM program-change numbers — not VST instances or their presets. PreSonus states its MIDI export does not capture program changes at all. The manual's own description of what is retained lists exactly three things: "All tempo information, tracks, and track names will be retained." Separately, the Studio One model is that an Instrument Track holds the performance data and the virtual instrument is a separate device: "The recorded data is the notes you played, not the sound of the instrument. Those notes can be edited and routed to any instrument for playback."
findings.practical: Expect to re-pick the sound after every import. That is not a loss — it is the point: I tell you "this line wants a violin, that one a horn", you assign the instrument in two clicks (next finding), and the sound choice stays your decision. Name your tracks in Studio One before exporting ("piano R", "bass"), because track names DO survive and they are how I know what I am looking at.

findings.claim: To change the instrument on a track that already has notes, drag a different instrument from the Browser onto that track and choose Replace.
findings.detail: The current Fender Studio Pro manual (Browser > Instruments and Effects Tabs) documents that dropping an instrument from the Browser onto an Instrument Track that already holds a virtual instrument brings up "a pop-up menu will appear, giving you the choice to Replace, Combine, or Keep the old instrument". Combine builds a Multi-Instrument (layering both); Keep leaves the old instrument and re-routes. Dropping into empty Arrange space instead loads the instrument into the Instruments Device Rack and creates a new Instrument Track routed to it. Instrument tracks are created with Track > Add Instrument Track. Fender's 8.2 press release additionally lists "Plug-in Replacement from the context menu" as new, but I could not retrieve a manual page or step list for it.
findings.practical: This is your "play it on piano, hear it as a violin" move, and it is two seconds: Browser (F5-ish, right-hand pane) > Instruments tab > drag e.g. Presence XT violin preset onto the piano track > click Replace. Your notes do not move. Use Combine when you want piano AND strings together.

findings.claim: You import a .mid back by dragging it from Explorer (or the Browser's Files tab) into the arrange area.
findings.detail: PreSonus MIDI FAQ documents drag-and-drop as the import route, with one trap: "Studio One uses a threshold for MIDI files, perhaps around 50kb in size, where if a MIDI file is over that threshold it will not import in to an existing song, but instead will create a new song". You can check beforehand — the bottom of the Browser shows preview controls when the file will merge into the current song. To force a new song deliberately: "drag and drop it anywhere except the arrange space. For example, drag and drop it to the main toolbar and it will open as a new song." You can expand the MIDI file's folder icon in the Browser to see its individual tracks and drag in only the ones you want (Type 1 only; Type 0 has no separate tracks). A Studio One 3.5-era community answer says File > Open also accepts .mid (File > Import being for audio/media) — unverified for current versions.
findings.practical: Drag the .mid I give you straight onto empty space below your existing tracks in the arrange view. Keep the files I return small and single-purpose (drums only, bass only) so you stay under the ~50 KB threshold and it merges instead of hijacking a new session. If a drop unexpectedly opens a new window, that threshold is why.

findings.claim: Importing a .mid into an existing song also brings its tempo in.
findings.detail: PreSonus's FAQ and a Vi-Control thread agree it does not: a reply there explains that dragging a MIDI file into the arrangement will not import tempo changes into the existing song, and the fix is to drag the MIDI file onto the Tempo Track. PreSonus's own FAQ describes the same deliberate action: "select a MIDI file in the browser Files tab and drag it directly to the Tempo Track in Studio One" to extract its tempo map. The forum part of this is user-reported, not documentation.
findings.practical: This is actually what you want: your session BPM stays put and my file snaps to your grid. So tell me the BPM once (or let the Save As… export tell me), and I will always return files at that same BPM. Only drag onto the Tempo Track if you deliberately want to adopt a different tempo map.

findings.claim: Bounce Selection / Ctrl+B is how you export a part.
findings.detail: Bounce renders to AUDIO, not MIDI. Manual: "To quickly bounce any Instrument Part to an Audio Track, select the Instrument Part, and then select Bounce Selection in the Event menu or simply press [Ctrl]/[Cmd]+[B]". PreSonus's own article describes "Bounce Selection" as rendering "the selected Instrument Part to a new Audio Event". You can also drag an Instrument Part directly onto an Audio Track and it is rendered to audio at that position.
findings.practical: Easy mistake to make with the keyboard shortcut right there. Ctrl+B gives me a WAV I can only listen to, not notes I can edit. Use right-click > Export Selection > Standard MIDI file instead. (Bouncing IS the right move at the very end, when you want the final audio.)

findings.claim: An MCP connection could let the assistant drive Studio One directly.
findings.detail: Two unofficial community MCP servers exist, both third-party, neither from PreSonus/Fender. FenderStudioProMCP (listed on glama.ai) states outright that Studio One has no public remote-control API and works around it: its MIDI-based command path "never reliably worked" and was replaced by driving the Ctrl+K command palette from a catalog built out of Studio One's keyboard-shortcut export; it is described as a work in progress, tested on Studio One 7 on macOS. A second project reads .song files and controls a running instance (mixer, transport, tracks, markers, ~1000 commands) through an in-app bridge device. I did not inspect either project's code or confirm Windows or version-8 support.
findings.practical: Do not build your workflow on this yet: no official API, alpha-quality projects, one tested only on macOS/v7, and any such bridge would have to run on YOUR PC — this session is in a Linux cloud container and cannot reach it. Revisit in a few months. The file hand-off below needs no software at all and works today.

findings.claim: The assistant can read a Windows folder path if the user supplies it.
findings.detail: This session runs in a Linux cloud container with no route to the user's machine; a path like C:\Users\...\piano.mid means nothing here. Anthropic's own in-session guidance for this environment: the session "runs in a cloud container and cannot reach their computer", and the way to work on local files is a session that runs on the machine — the Claude Desktop app, or `claude remote-control` run in a terminal inside the folder to work in, which then appears in the Claude Code app. The container does already hold the working tooling at /home/user/-/compose/compose.py, which takes a .mid path and an --out folder.
findings.practical: Two options. (a) Simplest, zero setup: attach the .mid to the chat. I read it directly, run the analysis, and hand back new .mid files you download and drag into Studio One. (b) If you want me to read a folder on your PC and write files straight back into it, run `claude remote-control` in that folder once — then the Studio One export folder becomes a path I can actually open, and the round trip loses the upload/download step.

findings.claim: Version context for the user's three installs.
findings.detail: Studio One Pro 7 was announced 14 October 2024 (KVR), adding stem separation, Splice integration, the Launcher, Deep Flight One and Impact upgrades; PreSonus said v7 would be the last numbered release before moving to time-based feature updates, and simplified the line to a single $199 tier plus a Pro+ subscription ($19.99/month). PreSonus support articles title v6 as "Studio One 6" and v7 as "Studio One Pro 7", so "Pro" entered the name at 7, and "Fender" at 8. The MIDI export/import commands quoted above come from the v6/v7 manual and the Browser Replace/Combine/Keep behaviour from the v8 Fender manual — i.e. the file-level workflow is unchanged across 6, 7 and 8.
findings.practical: Do all of this in Pro 8, your current install. The same clicks work in 7 and 6 if you ever open an old project there; only "Song" vs "Session" wording differs.

research.recommendation:
THE LOOP, click by click. Use the upload route (no setup); switch to remote-control later only if the upload step annoys you.

A. Play it yourself (Fender Studio Pro 8, your PC)
1. Track > Add Instrument Track. Drag a piano from Browser > Instruments onto it.
2. Double-click the track name and rename it something I can read: "piano RH", "bass", "drums". Track names are the ONLY labelling that survives a MIDI export, so this one step saves the most confusion later.
3. Set the BPM in the transport before you play, not after. Record your piano part (both hands is fine — I separate the top line from the chords underneath automatically).

B. Hand it to me
4. Whole arrangement: File > Save As… > set the file-type selector to *.mid > Save. This is the only export that keeps tempo + all tracks + track names. (There is NO File > Export > MIDI File — that path gives audio only.)
   Just the part you played: click the part > right-click > Export Selection > file type "Standard MIDI file" (not Musicloop) > Save.
5. Attach that .mid to the chat. Do not paste a C:\ path — this session is a Linux cloud container and cannot see your disk.

C. What I do
6. I read the notes, report key / scale / chord per bar / range, say which instrument each line actually suits and why, and write drum A/B/C, bass A/B/C and pad options locked to your bar grid at your BPM, each rendered to MP3 so you hear it before choosing. I never write your melody.
7. You get back one small .mid per element (drums.mid, bass.mid) plus previews.

D. Bring it back in
8. Drag each .mid from Explorer onto empty space below your tracks in the arrange view. Keep them small and single-purpose — a .mid over roughly 50 KB opens a NEW session instead of merging, which is the one real trap here.
9. Tempo: it does not import, by design — your session BPM wins and my file lands on your grid. Correct behaviour, not a bug.
10. Pick the sound: Browser > Instruments tab > drag the instrument you want onto the imported track > click Replace in the pop-up (Combine layers both instead). Your notes do not move. This is the "I played piano, I want violin" move, and it is the answer to "should Claude re-render it?" — no. Changing it in Studio One is two clicks and keeps the decision yours; me re-rendering only makes sense when the NOTES need to change (register, voicing, rhythm), not the timbre.
11. When a part is finished, Ctrl+B (Bounce Selection) renders it to audio. Only at the end — Ctrl+B earlier in the loop gives me a WAV I cannot edit.

Repeat B-D per element. One element per round keeps files small and keeps every choice traceable to you.

Two caveats worth saying plainly. The drag-a-part-into-the-Browser export works but the modifier key for "MIDI instead of Musicloop" is documented as Alt in the manual and as Shift in Fender's own feedback tracker, and Musicloop trims leading silence — so use Save As… / Export Selection instead and skip that ambiguity entirely. And an MCP bridge into Studio One is not ready: the only projects are unofficial, one states Studio One has no public remote-control API and drives the Ctrl+K palette as a workaround, tested on v7/macOS — and any bridge would have to run on your machine, which this session cannot reach.

On authorship (not legal advice): the melody and the A/B/C choices are yours and the record of them is what makes the piece yours; my accompaniment proposals are machine-generated material you select from and edit. Keep the exported .mid of what you actually played, dated, as your own evidence — that file is the thing that shows a human performance at the origin.

verdicts.claim: Studio One was rebranded by Fender; the product is now "Fender Studio Pro", effective 13 January 2026.
verdicts.reason: Holds against independent sources. MusicTech ("PreSonus Studio One Pro becomes Fender Studio Pro"), Production Expert and Mixdown all corroborate Sound On Sound: from 13 January 2026 Studio One becomes Fender Studio Pro, Quantum/AudioBox interfaces become Fender Quantum Series / Fender AudioBox, PreSonus retains studio monitors, PA speakers and digital consoles, and Fender acquired PreSonus in November 2021. The fenderstudiopromanual.fender.com host is confirmed real — search returns live pages from it (Mixing_Down.htm, Export_Stems_from_your_Session.htm, Instruments_and_Effects_Tabs.htm, Advanced_Options.htm). Two sub-details are NOT independently verifiable: the MyPreSonus-to-MyFender account migration (no source found) and the in-app path "Help > Studio Pro Reference Manual". I also could not confirm the older manual is still live at s1manual.presonus.com — every presonus.com and fender.com host is blocked by this container's egress policy (403 on CONNECT), so I verified via search snippets only.
verdicts.corrected_value: Rebrand date, hardware renames and PreSonus-retained lines confirmed. MyPreSonus→MyFender and the Help menu path: unverified. Extra confirmed detail from the SOS review: the Project Page was also renamed the Mastering Page in Pro 8.

verdicts.claim: The installed version is Fender Studio Pro Pro 8, build 8.2.0.114903.
verdicts.reason: The "unverifiable" status is correct and survives a second attempt. 8.2 itself is confirmed by two further sources: Mix Online ("Fender Studio Pro 8.2 Update Arrives", 21 Oct 2026) and Production Expert, both dating Fender's announcement to 20 October 2026 and listing Trim Automation, Dim Solo Mode, Multiple Marker Tracks, extended Stem Separation (guitar and piano), Vocal Tune Low Latency Mode, Per Note Sound Variations and MIDI 2.0. The four-part build string 8.2.0.114903 appears in no source I can reach, so it stays unconfirmed. The Wikipedia staleness claim is confirmed: its infobox gives 8.0.2 (3 March 2026). The Windows MIDI 2.0 caveat is also confirmed, and more sharply than the finding states.
verdicts.corrected_value: Windows MIDI 2.0 caveat confirmed and worth stating more plainly to the user: Production Expert reports MIDI 2.0 works on macOS now, while "Windows users will have to wait for Microsoft's official MIDI 2.0 release, which Fender says will require Windows 11 25H2 or later." So on this user's Windows machine MIDI 2.0 is effectively not yet usable — not merely version-gated. Irrelevant to the MIDI file workflow either way.

verdicts.claim: In version 8, a "Song" is now called a "Session".
verdicts.reason: Confirmed by a source independent of the two cited. Sound On Sound's own Fender Studio Pro 8 review states the terminology change directly: "it's no longer about 'songs', it's now all about 'sessions'", and adds that the Project Page was renamed the Mastering Page. The Fender manual corroborates it structurally — its pages are titled "Export Stems from your Session" and the Export Mixdown page refers to "the Mixdown folder for your Session". Owsinski's point that Pro 8 opens earlier PreSonus songs is also corroborated by the SOS review. No source gives a reason for the rename, so that part of the finding stands too.

verdicts.claim: MIDI is exported with File > Export > MIDI File.
verdicts.reason: Refuted, and the finding's own reasoning needs a correction. No source documents any File > Export > MIDI File item. PreSonus's Knowledge Base independently confirms the real route: use File > Save As... and select *.mid or *.midi in the export dialog's file format selector, and "some of the other export methods do not capture all of that data". But the finding's supporting line "File > Export in Studio One is for media/audio" is itself wrong: there is no File > Export submenu. The Fender manual's Mixing Down page says to "navigate to Session/Export Mixdown or press [Ctrl]/[Cmd]+[E]", and Export Stems sits in the same menu — i.e. the audio export commands live under the Session menu (the Song menu in v6/v7), not under File. The Export Stems page lists only Wave, AIFF, FLAC, CAF, Ogg Vorbis, M4A, AAC/ALAC and MP3, with no MIDI option, which supports the conclusion.
verdicts.corrected_value: Tell the user: MIDI leaves via File > Save As… (file-type selector to *.mid). Audio leaves via Session > Export Mixdown (Ctrl+E) or Session > Export Stems — the Song menu in v6/v7. There is no File > Export menu to look for at all.

verdicts.claim: File > Save As… to .mid exports the whole song (all tracks), not just selected ones, and keeps tempo and track names.
verdicts.reason: The load-bearing part holds. PreSonus's Knowledge Base independently confirms Save As to *.mid/*.midi as the route that carries the tempo map and song markers, where other export methods do not. Two details could not be independently verified because the manual host is blocked here: the exact sentence "All tempo information, tracks, and track names will be retained" and the existence of a "Convert To…" command — neither phrase appears in any source I can reach, so treat the track-names guarantee as documented-but-unconfirmed rather than proven. Nothing contradicts it.
verdicts.corrected_value: One practical caveat surfaced that the finding omits: because Save As exports the ENTIRE session, if the user wants only a couple of parts sent over they must mute or remove the rest first, or use the per-part export instead. Also, keep recommending they name tracks before export, since the name-retention claim is the one part still unverified — a quick test export will settle it.

verdicts.claim: You can export only the parts you select, via right-click > Export Selection.
verdicts.reason: The command exists and the headline claim holds, but two sub-claims are contradicted by a different source and should be softened. Sound On Sound's coverage of Export Selection says "a separate file is created for each selected event; no mixing of events occurs", that "Instrument parts are exported as Musicloop files" while audio events become WAVs, and that a mixed selection exports only one type. That conflicts with the finding's quoted "Multiple Instrument Parts can be exported at once to a single file" and with the claim that the dialog offers a Musicloop-or-Standard-MIDI-file choice. The SOS article is older and may predate a change, and I could not reach the manual to adjudicate, so this is an unresolved source conflict rather than a clean refutation.
verdicts.corrected_value: Do not promise the user that several selected parts land in one .mid. Tell them Export Selection is reliable for ONE part, and that if they want several parts in a single file they should use File > Save As… instead. Also warn that older documentation describes Export Selection producing Musicloops for instrument parts, so they should check the file-type selector in the dialog and pick Standard MIDI file if offered.

verdicts.claim: Dragging a part into the Browser exports it; hold Alt to get a MIDI file instead of a Musicloop.
verdicts.reason: Not independently verifiable on the key point, and the finding's own hedging is appropriate. Sound On Sound confirms the drag-export exists and that dragging to the Files tab produces a Musicloop which retains the loaded instrument and effects settings, and separately that dragging a MIDI clip into the Browser saves it to disk. But no source I can reach confirms the modifier: the only corroboration is a KVR user who recalls that "you'd need to hold down the Alt (Opt) key while dragging, but I don't remember which" operation — an explicitly unreliable recollection — and nothing mentions Shift. The Musicloop-trims-leading-silence risk is also unverified.
verdicts.corrected_value: Keep this as the finding already frames it: a convenience, not the reliable path. The modifier key is genuinely undocumented in anything I can verify, so the user should expect to experiment, and the recommendation to prefer Save As… or Export Selection is the right call.

verdicts.claim: Studio One writes Type 1 (multitrack) MIDI files only.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed. PreSonus's MIDI FAQ states it directly — "Studio One only exports Type 1 (multitrack) MIDI files, not Type 0" — and the statement reappeared consistently across multiple independent searches of that Knowledge Base. The companion limitation is confirmed from the same source: "Studio One doesn't capture program changes in it's MIDI file exports." The finding's caution that PreSonus flags the article as possibly out of date is appropriate, but nothing contradicts either statement, and the practical consequence for this workflow (separate, individually named tracks arriving in the analysis) is unaffected.

verdicts.claim: Instrument assignments survive the MIDI round trip.
verdicts.reason: Refuted, and corroborated from a second direction. PreSonus's own FAQ confirms Studio One does not capture program changes in MIDI exports, so not even GM program numbers survive. Avid's Pro Tools manual independently documents the same format-level limit in another DAW — MIDI export does not preserve device assignments — confirming this is inherent to Standard MIDI Files, not a Studio One quirk. The Studio One architecture point also holds: the Fender manual's Browser page treats the virtual instrument as a separate device that an Instrument Track is merely routed to, which is why dropping a new instrument on a track re-points the same notes at a different sound.
verdicts.corrected_value: The practical advice is right and important: the user must re-pick the sound after every import, and should name tracks in Studio One before exporting, since track names are the only labelling that has any chance of surviving.

verdicts.claim: To change the instrument on a track that already has notes, drag a different instrument from the Browser onto that track and choose Replace.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed, with the three options' exact semantics corroborated. The Fender Studio Pro manual's Instruments and Effects Tabs page documents that dragging an instrument from the Browser onto an Instrument Track already routed to another virtual instrument raises a pop-up with Replace (swaps the old instrument out of the Instrument panel), Combine (puts both into a new Multi Instrument) and Keep (re-routes the track to the new instrument, leaving the old one in the panel). A Future Music article independently describes the Combine route producing a "flexible 'multi-instrument' setup". The empty-arrange-space behaviour is also confirmed: the instrument loads into the Instruments Device Rack and a new Instrument Track routed to it is created. Fender's 8.2 "Plug-in Replacement from the context menu" is confirmed as a listed 8.2 feature but still has no retrievable step list.
verdicts.corrected_value: Minor: drop the vague "(F5-ish)" hint for the Browser — no source confirms that key. Note also that Keep, not just Combine, leaves the old instrument loaded, which matters if the user wonders why CPU use did not drop.

verdicts.claim: You import a .mid back by dragging it from Explorer (or the Browser's Files tab) into the arrange area.
verdicts.reason: The drag-import route is confirmed, but the finding's load-bearing operational detail — the ~50 KB threshold — is refuted for every version this user owns, and it drives advice that would waste their time. PreSonus's Studio One 6 MIDI FAQ states the size limit for adding MIDI files to existing songs has been removed, so a file of any size can be dropped into an existing song without opening a new one. The Studio One 6.0.1 release notes (November 2022) independently record the removal of the MIDI import file-size cap, with a follow-up fix in 6.0.2. The finding sourced the threshold from the older FAQ that PreSonus itself flags as possibly out of date. The same obsolete article is also the source of the claim that even dragging a single track out of a Type 1 file opens the whole file as a new song — which contradicts the finding's own advice to expand the folder icon and drag individual tracks; both tensions dissolve once the cap is gone.
verdicts.corrected_value: Drop the file-size rule entirely for v6/7/8: the ~50 KB threshold was removed in Studio One 6.0.1 (Nov 2022). Return files at whatever size the arrangement needs — drums and bass together is fine. Keep the drag-onto-empty-arrange-space instruction, and keep the deliberate "drop onto the main toolbar to open as a new song" trick, both still documented.

verdicts.claim: Importing a .mid into an existing song also brings its tempo in.
verdicts.reason: Refuted. PreSonus's Knowledge Base documents the Tempo Track drag as the deliberate, separate action needed to extract a MIDI file's tempo map, which only makes sense if a normal arrange-area drop does not import tempo. The VI-Control thread corroborates it from the user side. Searches surfaced the same conclusion repeatedly and nothing contradicted it. A further independent data point: a Reddit r/StudioOne user reports there is no simple way to export the tempo map on its own, consistent with tempo being handled through the Tempo Track rather than ordinary MIDI import.
verdicts.corrected_value: The practical framing is right and is the one the user should hear: session BPM stays put and returned files snap to their grid, so the assistant just has to return files at the user's BPM. Only drag onto the Tempo Track to deliberately adopt a different tempo map.

verdicts.claim: Bounce Selection / Ctrl+B is how you export a part.
verdicts.reason: Refuted from two further sources. A PreSonus Knowledge Base article confirms Ctrl+B / Cmd+B Bounce Selection on an instrument part creates a new audio track and places the rendered audio at the matching timeline position. Sound On Sound independently states each selected instrument part is rendered separately including insert effects from its instrument return channel, and that the source instrument parts are muted afterwards. Both describe audio output, so Ctrl+B cannot be used to hand over editable notes. One caveat on the finding's framing: a Steinberg-forum reply claims Bounce Selection is for audio events and that instrument tracks need Render In Place instead, so the exact command for rendering instruments may vary by version — but every source agrees the result is audio either way.
verdicts.corrected_value: Keep the warning. Add that bouncing also MUTES the source instrument parts, which is a surprise worth flagging — a user who presses Ctrl+B by mistake will find their piano part silent and may think it was deleted.

verdicts.claim: An MCP connection could let the assistant drive Studio One directly.
verdicts.reason: The claim holds and both projects are confirmed to exist via GitHub's API — a genuinely independent source from the glama listing. pajdarova/FenderStudioProMCP: Python, 12 stars, 2 forks, created 2026-08-07, last updated 2026-10-18, public, not archived, topics daw / fender-studio-pro / mcp-server / music. NeanderthalMan/studio-one-mcp: JavaScript, 12 stars, created 2026-09-28, last updated 2026-10-20, public, not archived, described as "MCP server for PreSonus Studio One: read .song files, and drive a running Studio One (mixer, transport, tracks, markers, ~1,000 commands) through an in-app bridge device" — matching the finding's second project exactly. Both are therefore real, third-party and currently maintained. However, the finding's MECHANISM detail for FenderStudioProMCP appears wrong: the glama listing describes it driving Studio One through four complementary push-based paths via a virtual MIDI port named StudioPro-MCU pinned to a fixed uniqueID, with an inventory of 194 built-in commands and 221 macros that the author plans to map to MIDI and expose as MCP tools — i.e. MIDI is the live mechanism, not an abandoned one, and no source mentions a Ctrl+K command palette or a keyboard-shortcut export catalog. I could not read either README directly: GitHub content access in this session is restricted to the user's own repository. "No public remote-control API" and "tested on Studio One 7 on macOS" are both corroborated; Windows and version-8 support remain unconfirmed.
verdicts.corrected_value: Keep the recommendation (do not build the workflow on this yet), but drop the Ctrl+K command-palette story — it is unsupported. Accurate description: FenderStudioProMCP drives Studio One over a virtual MIDI port (StudioPro-MCU) across several push-based paths, with ~194 built-in commands and ~221 macros catalogued; studio-one-mcp reads .song files and controls a running instance through an in-app bridge device. Both are alpha third-party work, both must run on the user's own PC, and neither is confirmed on Windows or on version 8.

verdicts.claim: The assistant can read a Windows folder path if the user supplies it.
verdicts.reason: Refuted, and I verified it directly rather than by citation. This container cannot resolve a single external hostname locally (DNS fails for every host tested) and all egress is forced through a policy proxy that returns 403 on CONNECT for the vendor documentation hosts — there is plainly no route to the user's machine, and a path like C:\Users\...\piano.mid is meaningless here. The in-session environment documentation confirms it in the same terms the finding quotes: this session "runs in a cloud container and cannot reach their computer", and the remedy is a session that runs on the machine — the Claude Desktop app, or `claude remote-control` in a terminal in the folder to work in, which then appears in the Claude Code app. I also confirmed the local tooling exists: /home/user/-/compose/compose.py (25,546 bytes) alongside /home/user/-/compose/midi_theory.py, invoked as `compose/compose.py <your>.mid --out <folder>`, documented as reading the user's MIDI without changing it and proposing accompaniment only.
verdicts.corrected_value: Both options are correct as written. Worth adding for this user's copyright requirement: compose.py's own header states it never invents a melody — only accompaniment is proposed and the user selects which proposal in decisions.json — which is exactly the human-authorship posture they asked for.

verdicts.claim: Version context for the user's three installs.
verdicts.reason: The substance holds but one date and one price are wrong. The official PreSonus press release introducing Studio One Pro 7 is dated 9 October 2024 (hosted on Fender's newsroom), with trade coverage following 14-15 October — so "announced 14 October 2024" is KVR's publication date, not the announcement date. Everything else is confirmed independently by Mix Online and ProSoundWeb: Stem Separation and the integrated Launcher as headline features; Pro 7 as the last release to hold features back for a major version number, with future updates arriving several times a year as feature releases; and the "Pro" naming arriving at 7 with "Fender" at 8. The claim that the file-level MIDI workflow is unchanged across 6, 7 and 8 holds in the sense that no source documents a change — but note it is partly inference, and the one genuine behavioural difference I found across versions is the MIDI import size cap removed at 6.0.1.
verdicts.corrected_value: Announcement date: 9 October 2024, not 14 October. Pricing per Mix Online: $199.99 perpetual (not $199), $149.99 upgrade from older Artist/Professional editions, $179.99 bundled with 12 months of Pro+, and Pro+ at $19.99/month. The "do all of this in Pro 8" advice stands.
